The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 
$$
{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime } = 𝒇 ( \mathbf{x} )
$$
where $\mathbf{x} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( t ) \\ y ( t )\end{array} \right]}$ and 
$$
𝒇 ( \mathbf{x} ) = \left[ \begin{array}{c}{x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 5 \\ {x}^{2} - {y}^{2} - 3\end{array} \right] .
$$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $𝒇 ( \mathbf{x} ) .$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{𝒇}^{\prime } ( \mathbf{x} ) = \left[ \begin{array}{cc}\frac{\partial  {f}_{1}}{\partial  x} & \frac{\partial  {f}_{1}}{\partial  y} \\ \frac{\partial  {f}_{2}}{\partial  x} & \frac{\partial  {f}_{2}}{\partial  y}\end{array} \right] .
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{array}{rlrl}\displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  {f}_{1}}{\partial  x}} & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{\partial }{\partial  x}} ( {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 5 ) = 2 x , \hspace{1em} & \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  {f}_{1}}{\partial  y}} & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{\partial }{\partial  y}} ( {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 5 ) = 2 y \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  {f}_{2}}{\partial  x}} & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{\partial }{\partial  x}} ( {x}^{2} - {y}^{2} - 3 ) = 2 x , \hspace{1em} & \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  {f}_{2}}{\partial  y}} & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{\partial }{\partial  y}} ( {x}^{2} - {y}^{2} - 3 ) = - 2 y\end{array}
$$

Thus, we have:

$$
{𝒇}^{\prime } ( \mathbf{x} ) = \left[ \begin{array}{cc}2 x & 2 y \\ 2 x & - 2 y\end{array} \right] .
$$

Now, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^\ast = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}$ to get

$$
{𝒇}^{\prime } ( {\mathbf{x}}^{∗} ) = \left[ \begin{array}{cc}4 & 2 \\ 4 & - 2\end{array} \right] .
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at $\mathbf{x}^\ast.$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:
$$
\begin{array}{cc}∣ \begin{array}{cc}4 - \lambda  & 2 \\ 4 & - 2 - \lambda \end{array} ∣ &  = 0 \\ ( 4 - \lambda  ) ( - 2 - \lambda  ) - ( 4 ) ( 2 ) &  = 0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} - 2 \lambda  - 16 &  = 0\end{array}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues
$$
{\lambda }_{1} = 1 - \sqrt{17} ,  {\lambda }_{2} = 1 + \sqrt{17} .
$$

Finally, since we have two real eigenvalues with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{unstable saddle}}.$

The Wronskian $W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})$ of two vector-valued functions 

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{11}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t)\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{22}(t)\end{bmatrix}
$$

is defined as

$$
W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=det({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=\begin{vmatrix}{x}_{11}(t) & {x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t) & {x}_{22}(t)\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Note the following:

- If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

- If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly dependent.

First, we write our system in matrix form:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 7 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

Now, let's substitute the given vectors into the matrix differential equation:

- $a(t)=\begin{bmatrix}7{e}^{-4t} \\ 2{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}(7{e}^{-4t})^{′} \\ (2{e}^{-4t})^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 7 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7{e}^{-4t} \\ 2{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-28{e}^{-4t} \\ -8{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-6\cdot 7{e}^{-4t}+7\cdot 2{e}^{-4t} \\ -2\cdot 7{e}^{-4t}+3\cdot 2{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-28{e}^{-4t} \\ -8{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-28{e}^{-4t} \\ -8{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $b(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{isn't}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}({e}^{t})^{′} \\ (-2{e}^{t})^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 7 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-6\cdot {e}^{t}+7\cdot (-2{e}^{t}) \\ -2\cdot {e}^{t}+3\cdot (-2{e}^{t})\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-20{e}^{t} \\ -8{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- $c(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}({e}^{t})^{′} \\ ({e}^{t})^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 7 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-6\cdot {e}^{t}+7\cdot {e}^{t} \\ -2\cdot {e}^{t}+3\cdot {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the set of solutions ${a,c}.$ Its Wronskian is

$$
\begin{aligned}W(a,c) & =\begin{vmatrix}7{e}^{-4t} & {e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-4t} & {e}^{t}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(7{e}^{-4t})\cdot {e}^{t}-{e}^{t}\cdot 2{e}^{-4t} \\  & =7{e}^{-3t}-2{e}^{-3t} \\  & =5{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}
$$

which is nonzero for at least one $t\in R.$ Thus, since $a$ and $c$ are both solutions of the same linear system, and their Wronskian is nonzero for at least one $t\in R,$ ${a,c}$ is a set of fundamental solutions of the system.

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =0,\,v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t+1 \\ t\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that ${x}_{E}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ are equilibrium solutions of the system since ${x}_{E}^{′}(t)=0.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′} &=f(x,y,z)\, && z(a)=d,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{″}+3y{y}^{′} & =2x \\ x{y}^{″} & =2x-3y{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{2x-3y{y}^{′}}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{2x-3yz}{x}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=-2.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(1)=0, \\ {z}^{′} &=\frac{2x-3yz}{x},\, && z(1)=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

Since we want to find the values of $y$ and ${y}^{′}=z$ at $x=\frac{5}{4},$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=\frac{5}{4}-1=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

First, we place the initial condition data in the table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $0$ |  |  | $-2$ |  |  |

Next, we compute both ${y}^{′}$ and ${z}^{′}$ according to the given rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=-2 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{2x-3yz}{x} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 1-3\cdot 0\cdot (-2)}{1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-2$ |  | $-2$ | $2$ |  |

Next, we compute $Δy$ and $Δz$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =(-2)\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-2$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $-2$ | $2$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

To get the new values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x,$ $Δy$ to $y,$ and $Δz$ to $z,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{5}{4} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=0+\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\frac{1}{2} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=(-2)+\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these values to our table in a new row gives the following:

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-2$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $-2$ | $2$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |
| $\frac{5}{4}$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ |  |  | $-\frac{3}{2}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)≈-\frac{1}{2}$
and
${y}^{′}\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)=z\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)≈-\frac{3}{2}.$

The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y \\ 1-{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y)=1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-{x}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-{x}^{2})=0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) & 1 \\ -2x & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi (1)) & 1 \\ -2(1) & 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda  & 1 \\ -2 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ -\lambda \cdot (-1-\lambda )-1\cdot (-2) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\text{i}.$

Finally, since we have two complex eigenvalues with negative real parts, our equilibrium is an $\text{asymptotically stable}$ $\text{spiral sink}.$

x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),

The Wronskian $W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})$ of two vector-valued functions

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{11}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t)\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{22}(t)\end{bmatrix}
$$

is defined as

$$
W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=det({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=\begin{vmatrix}{x}_{11}(t) & {x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t) & {x}_{22}(t)\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Note the following:

- If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

- If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly dependent. In this case, they do **not** form a fundamental set of solutions.

First, we write our system in matrix form:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}x(t).
$$

Now, let's substitute the given vectors into the matrix differential equation:

- $a(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}({e}^{3t})^{′} \\ ({e}^{3t})^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3t} \\ 3{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot {e}^{3t}+1\cdot {e}^{3t} \\ 1\cdot {e}^{3t}+2\cdot {e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3t} \\ 3{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3t} \\ 3{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $b(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{isn't}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}({e}^{t})^{′} \\ ({e}^{t})^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot {e}^{t}+1\cdot {e}^{t} \\ 1\cdot {e}^{t}+2\cdot {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- $c(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{3t} \\ 5{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{is}$ also a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}(5{e}^{3t})^{′} \\ (5{e}^{3t})^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{3t} \\ 5{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}15{e}^{3t} \\ 15{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 5{e}^{3t}+1\cdot 5{e}^{3t} \\ 1\cdot 5{e}^{3t}+2\cdot 5{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}15{e}^{3t} \\ 15{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}15{e}^{3t} \\ 15{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the set of solutions ${a,c}.$ Its Wronskian is

$$
\begin{aligned}W(a,c) & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{3t} & 5{e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t} & 5{e}^{3t}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =({e}^{3t})(5{e}^{3t})-(5{e}^{3t})({e}^{3t}) \\  & =5{e}^{6t}-5{e}^{6t} \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which is zero for all $t\in R.$ Thus, since $a$ and $c$ are both solutions of the same linear system, but their Wronskian is identically zero, they are linearly dependent and do **not** form a fundamental set of solutions of the system.

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{vmatrix}

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=\begin{vmatrix}2x & 2y \\ 2x & -2y\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =\begin{vmatrix}2(0) & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & -2(0)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is $\text{not almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+x \\ 2x+3y\end{bmatrix}.$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+x)=2x+1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+x)=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+3y)=2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+3y)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x+1 & 2y \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get 

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2(0)+1 & 2(0) \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalue of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(3-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=1,\text{ }3.$

Finally, since we both have two real and positive eigenvalues, our equilibrium is an $\text{unstable}$ $\text{source}.$

For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,{y}_{0}=y({x}_{0}),
$$

the implicit Euler method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

First, since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=-\frac{1}{2},$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=-\frac{1}{2}-(-1)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the implicit Euler method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & ={y}_{\text{new}}\cdot (({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}+1)\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}(({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy$ and solve for the general formula for ${y}_{\text{new}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}(({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}+1),\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}}-\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}(({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}+1) & =y \\ \frac{1}{2}(1-({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}){y}_{\text{new}} & =y \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{2y}{1-({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is ${x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=-1+\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}.$ Hence, the new $y$ value is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{2y}{1-({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 1}{1-{\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{8}{3} \\  & ≈2.67,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

Therefore, we conclude that $y\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)≈2.67.$

We will now complete our approximation of the value of $y(1)$ using the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method.

First, recall that we previously initialized with the RK4 method and completed the predictor step of the ABM $2$-step method, resulting in the following values:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ | $y'_p$ | $\Delta y$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ |  |  |

Now, the slope at the point $(x_\text{new},y_p) = \left(\dfrac12+\dfrac12, \dfrac{13}8\right) = \left(1, \dfrac{13}8\right)$ estimated by the predictor is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{'} & =4{x}_{\text{new}}-2{y}_{p} \\  & =4\cdot 1-2\cdot \frac{13}{8} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ | $y'_p$ | $\Delta y$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ | $\dfrac34$ |  |

Looking at the partially filled table, we note the following:

- From the second row, the slope at the current point $(x, y) = \left(\dfrac12, \dfrac34\right)$ is $y' = \dfrac12.$

- From the first row, the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y_{-1}) = \left(0, 1\right)$ is $y'_{-1} = -2.$

Finally, we compute $\Delta y$ using the corrector equation:

$$

Let's find $e^{At}$ for
$A =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}$
By solving the characteristic polynomial $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we can find that the eigenvalues of $A$ are $$ \lambda_1=2, \qquad \lambda_2=7. $$ We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\ & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ -7{\alpha }_{1}t & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned} $$ where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined. Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are $$ \lambda_1=2t, \qquad \lambda_2=7t, $$ both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}r(2t) &={e}^{2t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,\Rightarrow \,\left\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right. $$ Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$ - Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get $$ 5t\alpha_1 = e^{7t} - e^{2t} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \alpha_1 = \dfrac{1}{5t}\bigl(e^{7t}-e^{2t}\bigr). $$ - Multiplying the first equation by $7$ and subtracting twice the second one, we get $$ 5\alpha_0 = 7e^{2t} - 2e^{7t} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \alpha_0 = \dfrac{1}{5}\bigl(7e^{2t}-2e^{7t}\bigr). $$ Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following: $$ \begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t}) \\ & =\frac{1}{5}((2{e}^{7t}-2{e}^{2t})+(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t})) \\ & ={e}^{2t} \\ -7{\alpha }_{1}t & =-7(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t \\ & =-\frac{7}{5}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}) \\ & =\frac{7}{5}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{7t}) \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t}) \\ & =\frac{1}{5}((7{e}^{7t}-7{e}^{2t})+(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t})) \\ & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 7({e}^{2t}-{e}^{7t}) & 5{e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix} $$

Suppose a $2 \times 2$ system has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=0$ and $\lambda_2\neq 0$ with eigenvectors $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2.$

Then, the eigenvector direction for $\lambda_1=0$ gives a **line of equilibria**:

$$
\mathbf{x}_E = c_1 \mathbf{v}_1, \qquad c_1 \in \mathbb{R}
$$

The other eigenvalue $\lambda_2$ determines what happens off the equilibrium line:

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the equilibrium line (*unstable* direction).

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the equilibrium line (*stable* direction).

A typical solution has the form

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 e^{\lambda_2 t}\mathbf{v}_2,
\qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

So trajectories are *parallel to $\mathbf{v}_2,$* shifted by the equilibrium vector $c_1\mathbf{v}_1.$

To illustrate, let's consider the following example

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)-2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where we know the eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_1=0$ and $\lambda_2=3,$ with corresponding eigenvectors $\mathbf{v}_1 = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}$ and $\mathbf{v}_2 = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 1\end{array} \right]},$ respectively.

Recall that for $x'(t) = f(x),$ a point $x^\ast$ is an *equilibrium* if $f(x^\ast) = 0.$ Solutions starting at $x^\ast$ remain constant for all $t.$

Now, consider a system in the plane with variables $x(t)$ and $y(t){:}$
$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y) = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{f}_{1} ( x , y ) \\ {f}_{2} ( x , y )\end{array} \right]}
$$

A point $\mathbf{x}^\ast = (x^\ast, y^\ast)$ is an **equilibrium point** if $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast) = \mathbf{0}.$ Both components must be zero:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}^{∗},{y}^{∗}) &=0 \\ {f}_{2}({x}^{∗},{y}^{∗}) &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

If $\mathbf{x}(t_0) = \mathbf{x}^\ast,$ then $\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{x}^\ast$ for all $t.$ The state does not change.

**Note:** In the phase plane, $\mathbf{f}(x,y)$ represents velocity. At an equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^\ast,$ the velocity is $\mathbf{0},$ so trajectories starting there stay there forever.

For example, let's find the equilibrium points of the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=x-y \\ {y}^{′} &=x+y-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

- **Step 1:** Set the right-hand sides equal to zero.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y &=0 \\ x+y-2 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

- **Step 2:** Solve the system. From the first equation, $y = x.$ Substitute into the second:

$$
x + (x) - 2 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2x = 2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 1.
$$

Thus, $y = 1.$

Therefore, the system has a single equilibrium point $\mathbf{x}^\ast = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}.$

When a Fourier series represents a function $f$, it is often much easier to differentiate the series term-by-term than to recompute a brand-new Fourier series from scratch. 

However, term-by-term differentiation is only guaranteed to work when the underlying periodic function is sufficiently "well-behaved".

The theorem about **term-by-term differentiation of Fourier series** states the following:

Suppose that

$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+b_n\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)
$$

is a $2L$-periodic function which is

- piecewise smooth, and

- continuous.

Then, the Fourier series of $f'(x)$ can be obtained by differentiating term-by-term the Fourier series of $f(x){:}$

$$
f'(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} -\dfrac{n\pi a_n}{L}\sin\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)+\dfrac{n\pi b_n}{L}\cos\bigg(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\bigg)
$$

In other words, if $f(x)$ is the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ defined on $x \in [-L,L),$ then the Fourier series of $f'(x)$ can be obtained by differentiating term-by-term the Fourier series of $f(x)$ provided that

- $F(x)$ is continuous on $x \in (-L,L),$

- $F(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x \in (-L,L),$ and

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -L^+} F(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to L^-} F(x).$

**Note:** The constant term $\dfrac{a_0}{2}$ disappears after differentiating, since $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\!\left(\dfrac{a_0}{2}\right)=0.$

In the next slides, we will apply this theorem to a specific example to see how it works in practice.

$m^{2} + 9m + 14|= 0; m^{2}\underbrace{+ 7m + 2m}_{9m} + 14|= 0; m(m + 7) + 2(m + 7)|= 0; (m + 7)(m + 2)|= 0$
Applying the zero product rule, we have the following:
$\begin{bmatrix}m + 7 = 0 & ⇒m =-7 \\ m + 2 = 0 & ⇒m =-2\end{bmatrix}$

$r =-7ands =-2$

Applying the zero product rule, we have the following:
$\begin{bmatrix}m + 1 = 0 & ⇒m =-1 \\ m + 4 = 0 & ⇒m =-4\end{bmatrix}$

To find the radius of the circle, we draw radii from the center to each of the triangle’s vertices. This forms three identical isosceles triangles, each with a central angle of $120^\circ$, as shown below.

![](images/5c/5c053b3b368ffd379091b1b72c4701c3b77c0438394235a0abede8676043086c.png)

Now, we take one of these isosceles triangles and draw an altitude from the center to the opposite side. This divides the triangle into two right triangles with angles $30^\circ$, $60^\circ$, and $90^\circ$.

In each $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle:

- The length of the longer leg $x$, which is opposite the $60^\circ$ angle, is half of our equilateral triangle's side length:
$x = \dfrac{AC}{2} = \dfrac{27}{2} = 13.5$.
- The length of the hypotenuse is the radius $r$ of the circle.

Finally, in a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle, the longer leg is

$$
\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}
$$

times the length of the hypotenuse:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= r \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\
13.5 &= r \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\
r &= \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \cdot 13.5 \\
&= \frac{27}{\sqrt{3}} \\
&= \frac{27}{\sqrt{3}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} \\
&= \frac{27\sqrt{3}}{3} \\
&= 9\sqrt{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of the circle is $9 \sqrt{3} \: \text{ft}$.

Explanation:

To factor the left-hand side, we need two numbers that multiply to $4 \cdot (-15) = -60$ and add to $-17$. These two numbers are $-20$ and $3$, so we can factor the left-hand side as follows:

$4y^{2} - 17y - 15|= 0; 4y^{2}\underbrace{-20y + 3y}_{-17y} - 15|= 0; 4y(y - 5) + 3(y - 5)|= 0; (y - 5)(4y + 3)|= 0$

Applying the zero product rule, we have the following:

$\begin{bmatrix}y - 5 = 0 & ⇒y = 5 \\ 4y + 3 = 0 & ⇒y =-\frac{3}{4}\end{bmatrix}$

Therefore, we conclude that the **positive** solution to the given equation is $y = 5$.

First, recall that the parabola is symmetric about the vertical line passing through the vertex. Because $g(3) = g(9)$, the vertex is midway between $x_1 = 3$ and $x_2 = 9$.

So, the $x$-coordinate of the vertex is

$$
\begin{aligned}
h &= \frac{x_{1} + x_{2}}{2} \\
&= \frac{3 + 9}{2} \\
&= 6
\end{aligned}
$$

Since at the vertex, $g(h) = k$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
g(6) &= a(6)^{2} - 12(6) + c \\
k &= 36a - 72 + c
\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the parabola has vertex below the $x$-axis, $k < 0$, we have
$\begin{bmatrix}36a - 72 + c & < 0 \\ 36a + c & < 72\end{bmatrix}$.

Now, we check each statement:

- Statement I is false because $c$ does not always have to be negative. For example, if the parabola opens upward with $a = 1 > 0$, we get
$\begin{bmatrix}36(1) + c & < 72 \\ c & < 36\end{bmatrix}$,
which could be positive.
- Statement II is true. Since the parabola opens upward, we must have $a > 0$.
- Statement III is false because $c$ does not always have to be positive. For example, if the parabola opens upward with $a = 3 > 0$, we get
$\begin{bmatrix}36(3) + c & < 72 \\ c & < - 36\end{bmatrix}$,
which is negative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

Recall that by the factor theorem, if $(sx-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$, then

$$
x=\dfrac{r}{s}
$$

is a root of the polynomial.
Thus, since $2x -5m$ is a factor of our polynomial $p(x)$, we must have

$$
p\left(\dfrac{5m}{2}\right) = 0
$$

With that in mind, let's examine the given options in turn.

- Option I, $p(x) = 4x^{2}+2x+18m$, is not valid. Here, we have
$p\left(\frac{3c}{2}\right)|= 4\left(\frac{5m}{2}\right)^{2} + 2\left(\frac{5m}{2}\right) + 18m; = 25m^{2} + 5m + 18m; = 25m^{2} + 23m; = m(25m + 23)$.
This equals zero only at $m=0$ or $m=-\dfrac{23}{25}$, neither of which is a negative integer. ${\color{red}\times}$

*Option II,*

$$
p(x)=4x^{2}+2x+10m
$$

is not valid. Here, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
p\left(\frac{3c}{2}\right) &= 4\left(\frac{5m}{2}\right)^{2} + 2\left(\frac{5m}{2}\right) + 10m \\
&= 25m^{2} + 5m + 10m \\
&= 25m^{2} + 15m \\
&= 5m(5m + 3)
\end{aligned}
$$

This equals zero only at $m=0$ or

$$
m=-\dfrac{3}{5}
$$

neither of which is a negative integer. ${\color{red}\times}$

*Option III,*

$$
p(x)=4x^{2}+2x+20m
$$

is valid. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}
p\left(\frac{3c}{2}\right) &= 4\left(\frac{5m}{2}\right)^{2} + 2\left(\frac{5m}{2}\right) + 20m \\
&= 25m^{2} + 5m + 20m \\
&= 25m^{2} + 25m \\
&= 25m(m + 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

This equals zero only at $m=0$ or $m=-1$, and $m=-1$ is a negative integer. ${\color{darkgreen}\checkmark}$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

y = 4x^2 - 8x + 7
$$

where

4x^2 - 8x + 7 = m

A quadratic equation has two distinct real roots if the discriminant is positive: $\mathcal{D} > 0$.

First, rewrite the equation in standard quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}
4x^{2} - 8x + 7 &= m \\
4x^{2} - 8x + 7 - m &= 0 \\
4x^{2} - 8x + (7 - m) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following:

$$
a = 4, \qquad b = -8, \qquad c = 7 - m
$$

So, computing the discriminant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
D &= b^{2} - 4ac \\
&= (-8)^{2} - 4(4)(7 - m) \\
&= 64 - 112 + 16m \\
&=-48 + 16m
\end{aligned}
$$

For two distinct real solutions, we need $\mathcal{D} > 0{:}$
$\begin{bmatrix}-48 + 16m & > 0 \\ 16m & > 48 \\ m & > 3\end{bmatrix}$

Since $m$ must be an integer, we conclude that the least possible value is
$4$.

First, we notice that the function has three distinct roots, $x = -4$, $x = 0$, and $x = 3$.

Based on the graph, we can make the following conclusions about the multiplicities of the roots:

- The graph is *not* tangent to the $x$-axis at $x = -4$. Therefore, this root is simple (the multiplicity equals $1$).
- The graph touches the $x$-axis and reverses direction at $x = 0$. Therefore, this root has even multiplicity.
- The graph is *not* tangent to the $x$-axis at $x = 3$. Therefore, this root is simple (the multiplicity equals $1$).

Therefore, the equation we need to find has the form

$$
f(x) = a(x + 4)x^n(x - 3)
$$

where $n$ is an even natural number.

Of the given options, the following are similar to the form described above:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= \frac{1}{3}(x + 4)x^{2}(x - 3), \\
f(x) &= -\frac{1}{3}(x + 4)x^{2}(x - 3)
\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, we can notice that the value of the function at $x=1$ is negative, that is, $f(1) \lt 0$.

- For $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{3}(x + 4)x^2(x - 3)$, we have
$f(1)|= \frac{1}{3}(1 + 4)(1)^{2}(1 - 3); =-\frac{10}{3}; < 0$.
- For $f(x) = -\dfrac{1}{3}(x + 4)x^2(x - 3)$, we have
$f(1)|=-\frac{1}{3}(1 + 4)(1)^{2}(1 - 3); = \frac{10}{3}; ≮0$.

Therefore, we discard

$$
f(x) = -\dfrac{1}{3}(x + 4)x^2(x - 3)
$$

Consequently, the equation that could represent the graph shown is

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{3}(x + 4)x^2(x - 3)
$$

$-25 + 5k = 5k \Rightarrow -25 = 0$,
which is not true. Therefore, no solution arises from this case.

Thus, the only value that satisfies the equation $z(k) = 5k$ is

$$
k = \dfrac{5}{2}
$$

Symmetric data is characterized by values that occur with regular frequencies, forming a balanced, mirror-image shape around a central point.

In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are equal to the center of the data set. Otherwise, the mean is found by dividing the sum of all data values by the number of values, while the median is the middle value of the data set when the values are arranged in order from smallest to greatest.

With this in mind, we proceed to calculate the mean and median for each data set associated with each museum.

- North Museum data points are not ordered, so we order them first from smallest to largest:
$480,\: 500,\: 520, \: 540, \: 560$
This data set is symmetric and contains $5$ elements, which is an odd number, so the mean and median are both equal to the $3$rd element:
$\textrm{Mean}(N) = \textrm{Median}(N) = 520$
- South Museum data points are already ordered from smallest to largest:
$300, \: 480, \: 500, \: 510, \: 520$
This data set is not symmetric, so its mean is
$Mean(S)|= \frac{300 + 480 + 500 + 510 + 520}{5}; = \frac{2310}{5}; = 462$.
Since it contains $5$ elements, its median is the $3$rd element:
$\textrm{Median}(S) = 500$

Since North Museum has a higher mean and median than South Museum, both statements are true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II".

Symmetric data is characterized by values that occur with regular frequencies, forming a balanced, mirror-image shape around a central point.

In a symmetric distribution, the mean is equal to the center of the data set. Otherwise, the mean is found by dividing the sum of all data values by the number of values.

With this in mind, we proceed to calculate the mean for each data set.

- Data set $G$ is symmetric with $5$ values (an odd number), so its mean is the $3$rd data value in the list:
$\textrm{Mean}(G) = 58$
- Data set $H$ is not symmetric, so its mean is
$Mean(H)|= \frac{40 + 57 + 60 + 63 + y}{5}; = \frac{220 + y}{5}$.

Since the mean of the data set $G$ is the same as the mean of the data set $H$, we equate them and solve for $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
Mean(H) &= Mean(G) \\
\frac{220 + y}{5} &= 58 \\
220 + y &= 58 \cdot 5 \\
220 + y &= 290 \\
y &= 70
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $y$ is $70$.

When every data value is multiplied by a constant, each statistic responds as follows:

- For $19$ *different* values, there is exactly one middle value (the $10$th value) of $50$. Multiplying every value by $2$ will also scale the middle value by $2$. So, the median changes.
- The mean depends on every value, so multiplying every value by the same constant scales the mean by the same factor.If we denote the $19$ different totals by $t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_{19}$ and multiply each by $2$, then the new mean is:
$\frac{2t_{1} + 2t_{2} + ⋯ + 2t_{19}}{19}|= (2 \cdot (t_{1} + t_{2} + ⋯ + t_{19}))/(19); = 2 \cdot 50; = 100$
So, the mean also changes.
- The range depends only on the difference between the largest and the smallest values. Multiplying both by the same positive constant multiplies that difference by the same constant. Thus, the range is scaled by $2$, so it changes.
- The standard deviation measures the spread about the mean. Since every value (and thus the mean) is multiplied by $2$, each deviation from the mean is also multiplied by $2$; hence the variance scales by $4$ and the standard deviation by $2$.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None".

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution $y_c$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
2\frac{\textrm{d} y_c}{\textrm{d} x} + 4 y_c = 0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
y_c  = Ae^{-2x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution $y_p(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $8\cos(3x) - 2\sin(3x).$ So, we assume the particular solution to be 

$$
y_p(x) = \alpha \cos(3x) + \beta  \sin(3x),
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of $y_p$ gives

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y_p}{\textrm{d}x} =   - 3\alpha \sin(3x) +  3\beta \cos(3x).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute $y_p$ and $y_p'$ into the differential equation:

$$
2 ( - 3\alpha \sin(3x) +  3\beta \cos(3x)) + 4(\alpha \cos(3x)+ \beta  \sin(3x)) = 8 \cos(3x) - 2\sin(3x).
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(6\beta + 4\alpha)\cos(3x) + (-6\alpha + 4 \beta) \sin(3x) = 8 \cos(3x) - 2\sin(3x).
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}6\beta +4\alpha &=8\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)) \\ -6\alpha +4\beta &=-2\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha=\dfrac{11}{13}, \beta=\dfrac{10}{13}.$

Therefore, 

$$
y_p(x) =  \dfrac{11}{13}\cos(3x) + \dfrac{10}{13} \sin(3x).
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x) = y_c(x)+y_p(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y =  A e^{-2x} + \left(\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{11}{13} }\right)\cos(3x) 
+ 
\left(\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{10}{13} }\right) \sin(3x).
$$

The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $90\cos(6t)\,\textrm{V},$ a resistor with resistance $30\,\Omega,$ and a capacitor with capacitance $\dfrac1{150}\,\textrm{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I = \dfrac{\textrm d q}{\textrm d t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 30\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 30I = 30\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{\left(\dfrac1{150}\right)} = 150q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
90\cos(6t) = 30\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 150q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 5q = 3\cos(6t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_c}{\mathrm{d}t} + 5q_c = 0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
q_c(t) = Ae^{-5t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $6t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $6t,$ i.e.,

$$
q_p(t) = \alpha\cos(6t) + \beta\sin(6t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-6\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+6\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-6\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+6\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t))+5(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ (-6\alpha +5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+(5\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-6\alpha +5\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) \\ 5\alpha +6\beta &=3\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha = \dfrac{15}{61}, \beta = \dfrac{18}{61}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t) = q_c(t) + q_p(t) = Ae^{-5t} + \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $q_c(t) = Ae^{-5t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The function $q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to\infty,$ we have

$$
q(t)\approx q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state charge, in coulombs, is given by

$$
\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{15}{61}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{18}{61}\right)^2} \approx 0.38,
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
3\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}-6{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{2x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).$ So, we assume the particular solution to be 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
3(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))-6(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(-6\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+(-6\alpha -6\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).

$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+5{q}_{c}=0.

An $n$th-order differential operator $L$ is linear if it is of the following form:

$$
L(y)={f}_{n}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}y}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}+{f}_{n-1}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{n-1}y}{\text{d}{x}^{n-1}}+⋯+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

where each ${f}_{i}$ is a function of $x$ only. 

With that in mind, let's check each operator.

- Operator ${D}_{1}$ is linear. It is a second-order linear differential operator of the form

$$
{D}_{1}(y)={f}_{2}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

with ${f}_{2}=x,{f}_{1}=-2,$ and ${f}_{0}=0.$

- Operator ${D}_{2}$ is *not* linear. The coefficient of the first term is ${y}^{2},$ which depends on $y$ and therefore fails linearity.

- Operator ${D}_{3}$ is *not* linear. The last term contains the nonlinear term ${y}^{2},$ which fails linearity.

Therefore, the correct answer is ${D}_{1}(y)=x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ only.

$$

- ${a}_{n}({\lambda }_{1})$ are the coefficients produced by the method when $\lambda ={\lambda }_{1}.$

We are given that the indicial equation is $3{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda =0.$
Solving for the roots, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (3\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =0,\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The larger solution is ${\lambda }_{1}=\frac{2}{3}.$ Therefore, the first Frobenius series solution we take is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={x}^{2/3}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n}.
$$

With $\lambda =\frac{2}{3},$ the recurrence relation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{4}{(\frac{2}{3}+n)(3(\frac{2}{3}+n)-2)}\,{a}_{n-1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3n(n+\frac{2}{3})}\,{a}_{n-1} \\  & =\frac{4}{n(3n+2)}\,{a}_{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & \ne 0, \\ {a}_{1} & =\frac{4}{1(3\cdot 1+2)}\,{a}_{0}=\frac{4}{5}{a}_{0}, \\ {a}_{2} & =\frac{4}{2(3\cdot 2+2)}\,{a}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{4}{5}{a}_{0}=\frac{1}{5}{a}_{0},\end{aligned}

Matrix exponentials can be used for solving homogeneous systems of the form

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix.

For example, consider the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=5y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-5x(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get
$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 5 \\ - 5 & 0\end{array} \right]} \mathbf{x}(t),
$$
where $\mathbf{x}(t) = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( t ) \\ y ( t )\end{array} \right]}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 5 \\ - 5 & 0\end{array} \right]}.$

Recall that given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is some constant vector.

Since we have already seen how to compute the standard fundamental matrix, we will not repeat the calculation here. So, computing the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system, we get
$$
\Phi_0(t) = e^{At} = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}\cos   ( 5 t ) & \sin   ( 5 t ) \\ - \sin   ( 5 t ) & \cos   ( 5 t )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.$

**Note:** Recall that for the general solution of the ordinary differential equation $x'(t)=ax(t),$ we have 

$$
x'(t)=ax(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
x(t) = c \, e^{at}, 
\quad
c \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

Now, for the general solution of the matrix differential equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ we obtain 

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \, \mathbf{c},
\quad
\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^n.
$$

In the previous lesson, we focused on dilution problems in which the incoming solution contained none of the substance being modeled. In those cases, the rate at which the substance entered the container was zero.

In many practical situations, however, the incoming solution *does* contain some amount of the substance. When this happens,

- the rate of entry is no longer zero, and

- the resulting differential equation takes the form of a first-order linear differential equation.

For example, suppose a storage tank initially holds $650\,\textrm{L}$ of water containing $1\,300\,\textrm{g}$ of dissolved chlorine.

- A solution containing $20\,\textrm{g/L}$ of dissolved chlorine is pumped into the tank at a rate of $5\,\textrm{L/min}.$

- At the same time, the completely mixed water is drained out at a rate of $5\,\textrm{L/min}.$

To construct the model for the amount of chlorine $Q$ in the tank, we compare the rates of chlorine entering and leaving. The derivative 
$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}$
describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which chlorine enters the tank minus the rate at which chlorine leaves the tank.

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}}}
$$

We compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which chlorine enters the tank.

The rate of chlorine entering is the concentration times the flow rate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}})\cdot (5\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (5\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =100\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which chlorine exits the tank.

Since the volume remains constant at $650\,\textrm{L},$ the concentration in the tank is $\dfrac{Q}{650}\,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{L}}.$ So, the rate of chlorine exiting is

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(5\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{650}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(5\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{650}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{Q}{130}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The net rate of change $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_\text{in} - Q'_\text{out}$ is the difference between the rate in and the rate out. Combining this with the initial condition $Q(0) = 1\,300\,\textrm{g},$ we can state the complete initial value problem:

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = 100 - \dfrac{1}{130}Q
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{1}{130}Q = 100, \quad Q(0) = 1\,300\,\textrm{g}}
$$

In a first-order linear RC circuit driven by a sinusoidal voltage, the solution consists of a transient charge, which decays over time, and a steady-state charge, which oscillates with the same frequency as the input.

As time increases, the transient charge vanishes, leaving a steady-state charge that oscillates periodically and is independent of the initial condition.

To demonstrate, let's find the amplitude of the steady-state charge in the RC circuit below.

![](images/fc/fc700238d93fd6529c7113cd1a650e8c03d796e606afd4b655123cd04ed11cc7.png)

The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $20\cos(4t)\,\textrm{V},$ a resistor with resistance $50\,\Omega,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $\dfrac{1}{150}\,\textrm{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs:

$$
I = \dfrac{\textrm d q}{\textrm d t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 50\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 50I = 50\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{\left(\dfrac{1}{150}\right)} = 150q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
20\cos(4t) = 50\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 150q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 3q = \dfrac{2}{5}\cos(4t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_c}{\mathrm{d}t} + 3q_c = 0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
q_c(t) = Ae^{-3t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $4t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $4t,$ i.e.,

$$
q_p(t) = \alpha\cos(4t) + \beta\sin(4t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))+3(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ (-4\alpha +3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+(3\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & =\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-4\alpha +3\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ 3\alpha +4\beta &=\frac{2}{5}\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha = \dfrac{6}{125}$ and $\beta = \dfrac{8}{125}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
q_p(t) = \dfrac{6}{125}\cos(4t) + \dfrac{8}{125}\sin(4t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t) = q_c(t) + q_p(t) = Ae^{-3t} + \dfrac{6}{125}\cos(4t) + \dfrac{8}{125}\sin(4t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $q_c(t) = Ae^{-3t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The function $q_p(t) = \dfrac{6}{125}\cos(4t) + \dfrac{8}{125}\sin(4t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to\infty,$ we have

$$
q(t) \approx q_p(t) = \dfrac{6}{125}\cos(4t) + \dfrac{8}{125}\sin(4t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state charge is given by

$$
\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{6}{125}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{8}{125}\right)^2} =0.08\,\textrm{coulombs}.
$$

This amplitude represents the maximum magnitude of the oscillating steady-state charge on the capacitor.

Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega.$

The external force is $f(t)=4\cos(4t)+12\sin(4t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $4.$ Therefore,
$\omega = 4.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. $y_c = R\cos{(\omega t + \phi)} = R\cos{(4t + \phi)}$

2\. $y_c = R\sin{(\omega t + \phi)} = R\sin{(4t + \phi)}$

3\. $y_c =A\cos{\omega t} + B\sin{\omega t} = A\cos(4t) + B\sin(4t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega$ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
y_p(t)=t(C\cos(4t)+D\sin(4t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega=4$ into the differential equation, $y'' + \omega^2y = f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[8(D-2Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-8(C+2Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)]+16t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+12\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 8D\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-8C\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+12\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-\dfrac{3}{2}$ and $D=\dfrac{1}{2}.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
y_p(t) = -\dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t) + \dfrac{1}{2}t\sin(4t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y = R\cos{(4t + \phi)} - \dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t) + \dfrac{1}{2}t\sin(4t)$

2\. $y = R\sin{(4t + \phi)} - \dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t) + \dfrac{1}{2}t\sin(4t)$

3\. $y = A\cos(4t) + B\sin(4t) - \dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t) + \dfrac{1}{2}t\sin(4t)$

Only solutions I and II match the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=8\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 8I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{C} = \dfrac{q}{0.25} = 4q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=4\,\textrm{H}.$ Hence,

$$
V_L = 4\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
6\cos(2t)=8I+4q+4\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(8I+4q+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ -12\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =8\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4\,\frac{dq}{dt}+4\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t},$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2I}{\mathrm{d}t^2}+2\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}+I=-3\sin(2t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $I_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2I_c}{\mathrm{d}t^2} + 2\, \dfrac{\mathrm{d}I_c}{\mathrm{d}t}+ I_c=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
I_c(t)=Ae^{-t}+Bte^{-t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e.,

$$
I_p(t) = \alpha\cos(2t)+\beta\sin(2t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+2(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ +(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ (-3\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+(-4\alpha -3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3\alpha +4\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ -4\alpha -3\beta &=-3\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha=\dfrac{12}{25}$ and $\beta=\dfrac{9}{25}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
I_p(t)=\dfrac{12}{25}\cos(2t)+\dfrac{9}{25}\sin(2t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t) = I_c(t) + I_p(t) = Ae^{-t} + Bte^{-t} + \dfrac{12}{25}\cos(2t) + \dfrac{9}{25}\sin(2t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $I_c(t) = Ae^{-t} + Bte^{-t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The function $I_p(t) = \dfrac{12}{25}\cos(2t) + \dfrac{9}{25}\sin(2t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to\infty,$ we have

$$

The external force is $f(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $1.$ Therefore,

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡t+D\operatorname{sin}⁡t).
$$

$$

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.

Therefore, the correct answer is $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ only.

The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $5\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $10\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.2\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $5\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=10\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=10I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.2}=5q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=5\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=5\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
5\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)=10I+5q+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(10I+5q+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ -15\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =10\,\frac{dI}{dt}+5\,\frac{dq}{dt}+5\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+I=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $3t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $3t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+2(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ +(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ (-8\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+(-6\alpha -8\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-8\alpha +6\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ -6\alpha -8\beta &=-3\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{9}{50}$ and $\beta =\frac{6}{25}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{9}{50}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{6}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t}+\frac{9}{50}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{6}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=\frac{9}{50}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{6}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{9}{50}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{6}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(\frac{9}{50}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{6}{25}\right)}^{2}}=\frac{3}{10}.
$$

The angles $\pi $ and $\frac{\pi }{2}$ are quadrantal angles. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](images/79/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

Let's first consider the angle $\pi .$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\pi $ corresponds to the point $(-1,0).$

- Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}\pi =-1.$

- Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}\pi =0.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{tan}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{tan}\pi =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\pi }{\operatorname{cos}\pi }=\frac{0}{-1}=0.
$$

Now, let's consider the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$

- Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=0.$

- Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=1.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{cot}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cot}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}=\frac{0}{1}=0.
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\operatorname{tan}\pi +\operatorname{cot}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=0+0=0.
$$

Let ${a}_{n}=2-2n.$ If we compute the first few terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =2-2(1)=0 \\ {a}_{2} & =2-2(2)=-2 \\ {a}_{3} & =2-2(3)=-4,\end{aligned}
$$

and we notice that this is an arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=-2$ and first term ${a}_{1}=0.$ 

We can compute the $k$th partial sum of an arithmetic series using the formula

$$
{s}_{k}=\frac{k}{2}({a}_{1}+{a}_{k}).
$$

Since ${a}_{11}=2-2(11)=-20,$ we get

$$
{s}_{11}=\frac{11}{2}(0-20)=-110.
$$

So the eleventh partial sum of ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(2-2n)$ is equal to $-110.$

v:
Let's compute the first few partial sums:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{1} & =-\sqrt{3} \\ {s}_{2} & =-\sqrt{3}+(-\sqrt{3})=-2\sqrt{3} \\ {s}_{3} & =-\sqrt{3}+(-\sqrt{3})+(-\sqrt{3})=-3\sqrt{3} \\ {s}_{4} & =-\sqrt{3}+(-\sqrt{3})+(-\sqrt{3})+(-\sqrt{3})=-4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Looking at the sequence of partial sums, we can see that the formula for the $n$th partial sum is 

$$
{s}_{n}=-\sqrt{3}n.
$$

The sequence of partial sums is divergent:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{s}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }(-\sqrt{3}n)=-\infty 
$$

Therefore, the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\sqrt{3})$ is also divergent.

Let's recall the properties of convergent series:

- If ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent, then ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }K\cdot {a}_{n}=K\cdot {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is also convergent.

- If ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent and ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent, then ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent.

- If ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent, then ${\sum }_{n=k}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is also convergent.

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement:

- Statement I is true. Any constant multiple of a convergent series gives a convergent series.

- Statement II is false. Removing a finite number of terms from a convergent series gives a convergent series.

- Statement III is false. The sum of two convergent series is convergent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Notice that the given series is a geometric series because it is in the form $\sum a{r}^{n}.$ 

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

The first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=45(0.1)^{1}=4.5.
$$

 

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{45(0.1)^{2}}{45(0.1)^{1}}=0.1.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }45(0.1)^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{4.5}{(1-0.1)} \\  & =\frac{4.5}{0.9} \\  & =\frac{45}{9} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

We analyze each series in turn.

- First, we look at ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{n\sqrt[3]{{n}^{2}}}.$ Rewriting this series gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{n\sqrt[3]{{n}^{2}}} & =2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{n\cdot {n}^{2/3}} \\  & =2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{5/3}},\end{aligned}
$$

and this is a $p$-series with $p=\frac{5}{3}.$ Since $p>1,$ the series converges by the $p$-series test.

- For the second series, we have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3{n}^{4}}=\frac{1}{3}\cdot {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{4}}
$$

 
which is a $p$-series with $p=4.$ Since $p>1,$ the series is convergent.

- For the third series, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5\sqrt[3]{n}}{\sqrt{n}} & =5{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{n}^{1/3}}{{n}^{1/2}} \\  & =5{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{1/6}},\end{aligned}
$$

and this is a $p$-series with $p=\frac{1}{6}.$ Since $p\le 1,$ the series diverges by the $p$-series test.

Hence, the correct answer is "I and II only."

Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{3{n}^{n}}{(1+n)^{n}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\left(\frac{3{n}^{n}}{(1+n)^{n}}\right)}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt[n]{3}\,n}{1+n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt[n]{3}\,n}{n(\frac{1}{n}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt[n]{3}}{(\frac{1}{n}+1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{0+1} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{3}=1.
$$

Since $L=1,$ the root test gives no conclusion.

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy+{x}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) & =0 \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y+2x & =0 \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-(2x+y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2x+y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,0)$ is

\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(1,\,0)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{2x+y}{x}\right)}_{(1,\,0)} \\  & =-\frac{2\cdot 1+0}{1} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's recall the properties of convergent series:

- If ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent, then ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }K\cdot {a}_{n}=K\cdot {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is also convergent.

- If ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent and ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent, then ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent.

- If ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent, then ${\sum }_{n=k}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is also convergent.

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement:

- Statement I is false. Removing a finite number of terms from a convergent series gives a convergent series.

- Statement II is false. Any constant multiple of a convergent series gives a convergent series.

- Statement III is false. The sum of two convergent series is convergent.

The angles ${0}^{∘}$ and ${270}^{∘}$ are quadrantal angles. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](images/ed/edad8c833f65c54453fe40a326cbf9394c263213934447872b530a8e4fb86de1.png)

Let's first consider the angle ${0}^{∘}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle ${0}^{∘}$ corresponds to the point $(1,0).$

- Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}({0}^{∘})=1.$

- Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}({0}^{∘})=0.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{tan}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{tan}({0}^{∘})=\frac{\operatorname{sin}({0}^{∘})}{\operatorname{cos}({0}^{∘})}=\frac{0}{1}=0.
$$

Now, let's consider the angle ${270}^{∘}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle ${270}^{∘}$ corresponds to the point $(0,-1).$

- Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}({270}^{∘})=0.$

- Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}({270}^{∘})=-1.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{cot}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cot}({270}^{∘})=\frac{\operatorname{cos}({270}^{∘})}{\operatorname{sin}({270}^{∘})}=\frac{0}{-1}=0.
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\operatorname{tan}({0}^{∘})+\operatorname{cot}({270}^{∘})=0+0=0.
$$
