Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{3})=2x, & \,\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{3})=3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x & 3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

and ${f}^{′}$ at $a=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ is

$$
{f}^{′}(a)=\begin{bmatrix}2(2) & 3(1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{tan}⁡x)=\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡x},\, & \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{tan}⁡x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} & \operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\pi }{4} \\ 2\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$

$$
z-2=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1\end{bmatrix}(\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\pi }{4} \\ 2\end{bmatrix}).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

$$
2+4+1=7.
$$

Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}_{1}^{2}))=2{x}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}_{1}^{2}),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}_{1}^{2}))=0 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}_{2}^{2}))=0,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}_{2}^{2}))=-2{x}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}_{2}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}_{1}^{2}) & 0 \\ 0 & -2{x}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}_{2}^{2})\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{\pi } \\ \sqrt{\pi }\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
f(a)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,{f}^{′}(a)=\begin{bmatrix}-2\sqrt{\pi } & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The linear approximation of $f$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

Substituting $f(a),$ ${f}^{′}(a),$ and $a$ in the equation above, we obtain

$$
f(x)≈\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-2\sqrt{\pi } & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}(x-\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{\pi } \\ \sqrt{\pi }\end{bmatrix}).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

$$
-1+(-2\sqrt{\pi })+0=-1-2\sqrt{\pi }.
$$

$$

$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{y}}{m}=\frac{8}{10}=\frac{4}{5}.

For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y & {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{bmatrix},$ 
 we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡y & 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y & -{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(2,\frac{\pi }{2}).$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}(2,\frac{\pi }{2})=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.

$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}6x+6 & -4 \\ -4 & 12{y}^{2}+8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
H(1,0)=12\cdot 8-(-4)\cdot (-4)=80.
$$

For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}y\operatorname{sin}⁡(y-x) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)+y\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)\end{bmatrix},$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y\operatorname{sin}⁡(y-x),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)+y\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y).
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{sin}⁡(y-x))=-y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)+y\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y))=\operatorname{sin}⁡(y-x)+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y) \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{sin}⁡(y-x))=\operatorname{sin}⁡(y-x)+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)+y\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y))=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)-y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(y-x)+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(y-x)+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)-y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(\pi ,\pi ),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(\pi ,\pi )=\begin{bmatrix}-\pi  & \pi  \\ \pi  & -\pi \end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(\pi ,\pi )=(-\pi )\cdot (-\pi )-\pi \cdot \pi =0.
$$

Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}|}_{x=a}
$$

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}}_{x=a}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =2, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1\end{bmatrix}, & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

v:
If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Calculating $x$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\  & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{4\pi }{3}\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating $y$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\  & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{4\pi }{3}\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating $z$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\  & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $H$ are $(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4},-\frac{3}{4},-\frac{3}{2}).$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

From the above equations, we can express $\rho $, $\theta $, and $ϕ$ in terms of $x$, $y$, and $z$ as follows:

$$
\rho =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{y}{x},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\frac{z}{\rho }
$$

First, we find $\rho :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}^{2}+{\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{4}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $(x,y)=(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},-\frac{1}{2})$  lies in the third quadrant. So to find $\theta ,$ we first need to find the reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-\frac{1}{2}}{-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we add $\pi $ to the reference angle to get $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & ={\theta }_{R}+\pi  \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}+\pi  \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $ϕ$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}ϕ & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡\left(\frac{z}{\rho }\right) \\  & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the spherical coordinates of $K$ are $(\sqrt{2},\frac{7\pi }{6},\frac{3\pi }{4}).$

$$

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$

$$

Recall that the union of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *at least one* set:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for at least one}\,\,k\in I\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=-0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{-0.5}=\{-0.5\}\times [-0.5,0.5]=\{(-0.5,k)\,:\,k\in [-0.5,0.5]\}.
$$

This represents a vertical line segment from the point $(-0.5,-0.5)$ to the point $(-0.5,0.5)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](images/b7/b7793d85e02ccd05c55c34971c90be087d58274eabd21f46fe09f08ccd60797b.png)

$$

$$

v:
Recall that the union of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *at least one* set:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for at least one}\,\,k\in I\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[-0.5,0.5]\times \{0.5\}=\{(k,0.5)\,:\,k\in [-0.5,0.5]\}.
$$

This represents a horizontal line segment from the point $(-0.5,0.5)$ to the point $(0.5,0.5)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](images/50/509d3e8d3bce0b422cad7e7f02377468cacc0de3a4e45647c12fef15f2c9991f.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[-i,i]\times \{1-i\}=\{(k,1-i)\,:\,k\in [-i,i]\}
$$

is the horizontal line segment from the point $(-i,1-i)$ to the point $(i,1-i).$ 

![](images/21/21859c2ac02ba80d47672bf2fab25f7358feb921bc5b546c1e8c783c2819bea3.png)

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following triangle that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}:$

![](images/5b/5b5715ba2a1b71a9f5aef52882ed62ba2fe1610c143224914430f79fdc8f06b5.png)

We're given that $x=0$ is a stationary point of $f(x).$ We will use the second derivative test to classify this stationary point.

Calculating the first derivative for the function $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}+\frac{1}{10},$ we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={x}^{4}-2{x}^{3}.
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we get 

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=4{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}.
$$

Substituting $x=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0) & =4(0)^{3}-6(0)^{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second derivative is zero, we conclude that the test is inconclusive, we need to use the first derivative test.

Let's  find other stationary points. Solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{4}-2{x}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{3}(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =0,2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So we have two stationary points, $x=0$ and $x=2.$ Next, to determine whether these points are local maxima or minima, we use the first derivative test.

Let's choose the test points $x=-1,1,3$ and evaluate the first derivative at these points.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-1) & =(-1)^{3}(-1-2)=3>0 \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =(1)^{3}(1-2)=-1<0 \\ {f}^{′}(3) & =(3)^{3}(3-2)=27>0\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize the information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,0)$ | $0$ | $(0,2)$ | $2$ | $(2,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $-1$ |  | $1$ |  | $3$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ | min | $↗$ |

So, we conclude that $f(x)$ has a relative maximum at $x=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f(x)$ has a relative maximum at $x=0$” only.

Let's apply the candidates test step by step.

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)=x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get 

$$
1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0\,⟹\,x=\frac{2\pi }{3}+2\pi n,\,\,\,\frac{4\pi }{3}+2\pi n,
$$

where $n$ is an integer. We discard all solutions except $x=\frac{2\pi }{3}$ since it is the only value that belongs to the given interval.

So, the critical points are $x=\frac{2\pi }{3},$ and the endpoints $x=0,\pi $ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints).

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =0+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)=0 \\ f\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right) & =\frac{2\pi }{3}+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right)=\frac{2\pi }{3}+\sqrt{3}≈3.8 \\ f(\pi ) & =\pi +2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )=\pi ≈3.1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The greatest value is $f\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right)=\frac{2\pi }{3}+\sqrt{3},$ so the global maximum is $\frac{2\pi }{3}+\sqrt{3}.$

- The smallest value is $f(0)=0,$ so the global minimum is $0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “The global maximum value is $\frac{2\pi }{3}+\sqrt{3}$”; “The global minimum value is $0$” only.

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
{H}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-∇f({x}_{n}).
$$

So we're now solving the inequality $f(x)<0.$

The solutions to the equation $f(x)=0$ are $x=0,$ $x=-\frac{1}{3},$ $x=3$ and $x=4.$ These roots divide the number line into $5$ subintervals:

$$
(-\infty ,-\frac{1}{3}),\,(-\frac{1}{3},0),\,(0,3),\,(3,4),\,(4,\infty )
$$

Now, we construct a sign table with the list of the intervals on the top and the list of factors on the left. Filling in the sign table using the usual method, we get the following result:

|  | $(-\infty ,-\frac{1}{3})$ | $(-\frac{1}{3},0)$ | $(0,3)$ | $(3,4)$ | $(4,\infty )$ |

First, we rearrange the equation to isolate $\operatorname{cot}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{cot}⁡x+3 & =3+\operatorname{cot}⁡x \\ 3\operatorname{cot}⁡x & =0 \\ \operatorname{cot}⁡x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can't find an equivalent equation involving tangent, since this would lead to us dividing by $0:$

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{1}{0}=\text{undefined}
$$

However, we can instead find an equivalent equation using the fact that $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}:$

$$
\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}=0
$$

In this case, we can find the principal solution as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ x & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡0 \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value lies inside the desired domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

To find more solutions, we subtract integer multiples of $\pi $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-\pi  \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}-\pi  \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in ascending order, our solutions are $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

Let $p$ represent the profit on a single roll of the game. On each roll in the game, there are two possible outcomes:

- If rolling gives an odd number ($1$, $3,$ or $5$), the player loses $$2,$ so we have $p=-2.$

- If rolling gives an even number ($2$ or $4$), the player wins $$10,$ so we have $p=10.$

The probabilities for the outcomes are

$$
P(-2)=\frac{3}{5},\,P(10)=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

Let's summarize this in a table.  If $p$ is the profit (in dollars) on a single game, and $f(p)$ is the probability mass function for $p,$ then we have the following:

| $f(p)$ | $\frac{3}{5}$ | $\frac{2}{5}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $p$ | $-2$ | $10$ |

Therefore, the expected value of $p$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}E[p] & =(-2)\cdot f(-2)+10\cdot f(10) \\  & =(-2)\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)+10\left(\frac{2}{5}\right) \\  & =-\frac{6}{5}+\frac{20}{5} \\  & =\frac{14}{5} \\  & =2.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the expected profit is $$2.80.$

v:
To solve this inequality using the graphical method, we first need to move all of the terms to the left-hand side so that the right-hand side is $0.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}^{2}+21x & \ge 12 \\ 6{x}^{2}+21x-12 & \ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we want to find the values of $x$ for which the parabola $y=6{x}^{2}+21x-12$ lies **above** the $x$-axis or touches this axis. Let's find the roots of the parabola by factoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}^{2}+21x-12 & =0 \\ (6{x}^{2}-3x)+(24x-12) & =0 \\ 3x(2x-1)+12(2x-1) & =0 \\ (3x+12)(2x-1) & =0 \\ 3(x+4)(2x-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We see that the roots are $x=-4$ and $x=\frac{1}{2},$ and we can graph the parabola as follows:

![](images/38/38c1897ec93625527b48ec689fbd65e9a63056e033fa6a7a0c72473f1188e7ea.png)

Since we are interested in solving 

$$
6{x}^{2}+21x-12\ge 0,
$$

 

we look for the part of the parabola that is **above** the $x$-axis or touches this axis. 

Based on the graph, the solution is $x\le -4$ or $x\ge \frac{1}{2}.$

Using interval notation, we write $x\in (-\infty ,-4]⋃[\frac{1}{2},\infty ).$

A reciprocal function is defined for all values of $x$ except for those that make the denominator zero. So, to find the domain, we must exclude all values of $x$ that make the denominator zero.

Setting the denominator equal to zero and solving, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8x-20 & =0 \\ 8x & =20 \\ x & =\frac{20}{8} \\ x & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is $x\in (-\infty ,\frac{5}{2})\cup (\frac{5}{2},\infty ).$

First, let's simplify the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}36{x}^{2} & >49 \\ {x}^{2} & >\frac{49}{36}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use either of two methods to solve the inequality.

*Method 1 - Solving an Absolute Value Equation*

Taking the square root of both sides of the inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{x}^{2}} & >\sqrt{\frac{49}{36}} \\ |x| & >\frac{7}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the definition of absolute value, we must have 

$$
x<-\frac{7}{6}\,\text{or}\,x>\frac{7}{6}.
$$

So, the solution is $x\in (-\infty ,-\frac{7}{6})\cup (\frac{7}{6},+\infty ).$

*Method 2 - Picturing a Quadratic Curve*

Starting from ${x}^{2}>\frac{49}{36}$ and moving all terms to the left-hand side, we reach

$$
{x}^{2}-\frac{49}{36}>0.
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding parabola given by $\,y={x}^{2}-\frac{49}{36}\,$ and find its roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-\frac{49}{36} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-{\left(\frac{7}{6}\right)}^{2} & =0 \\ (x-\frac{7}{6})(x+\frac{7}{6}) & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

so the roots are  $x=\pm \frac{7}{6}.$ 

Since the leading coefficient of ${x}^{2}-\frac{49}{36}$   is positive, the parabola opens upward. Hence, the solution set to the given inequality ($y>0$) lies outside the roots and does not include them:

Therefore, the solution is 

$$
x\in (-\infty ,-\frac{7}{6})\cup (\frac{7}{6},\infty ).
$$

First, we define the function $f(x)$ as

$$
f(x)=(3x-4)(1-x)(x+2).
$$

So we're now solving the inequality $f(x)>0.$

The solutions to the equation $f(x)=0$ are $x=-2,$ $x=1,$ and $x=\frac{4}{3}.$ These roots divide the number line into $4$ subintervals: 

$$
(-\infty ,-2),\,(-2,1),\,(1,\frac{4}{3}),\,(\frac{4}{3},\infty )
$$

Now, we construct a sign table with the list of the intervals on the top and the list of factors on the left. Filling in the sign table using the usual method, we get the following result:

|  | $(-\infty ,-2)$ | $(-2,1)$ | $(1,\frac{4}{3})$ | $(\frac{4}{3},\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $3x-4$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $1-x$ | $+$ | $+$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $x+2$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $f(x)$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ |

Finally, to solve the inequality $f(x)>0,$ we look at the bottom row to determine where $f(x)$ is positive.

From the table, we see that $f(x)$ is positive on the intervals $(-\infty ,-2)$ and $(1,\frac{4}{3}).$ 

Therefore, we conclude that $f(x)>0$ for all $x\in (-\infty ,-2)⋃(1,\frac{4}{3}).$

First, we define the function $f(x)$ as

$$
f(x)=(x+2)(2x-1)(1-x)(3x-4)(x-5).
$$

So we're now solving the inequality $f(x)\le 0.$

The solutions to the equation $f(x)=0$ are $x=-2,$ $x=\frac{1}{2},$ $x=1,$ $x=\frac{4}{3},$ and $x=5.$ These roots divide the number line into $6$ subintervals:

$$
(-\infty ,-2),\,(-2,\frac{1}{2}),\,(\frac{1}{2},1),\,(1,\frac{4}{3}),\,(\frac{4}{3},5),\,(5,\infty )
$$

Now, we construct a sign table with the list of the intervals on the top and the list of factors on the left. Filling in the sign table using the usual method, we get the following result:

|  | $(-\infty ,-2)$ | $(-2,\frac{1}{2})$ | $(\frac{1}{2},1)$ | $(1,\frac{4}{3})$ | $(\frac{4}{3},5)$ | $(5,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $2x-1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $1-x$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $x+2$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $3x-4$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $x-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $f(x)$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ |

Finally, to solve the inequality $f(x)\le 0,$ we look at the bottom row to determine where $f(x)$ is negative.

From the table, we see that $f(x)\le 0$ on the intervals $(-2,\frac{1}{2})$, $(1,\frac{4}{3})$, and $(5,\infty ).$

Therefore, remembering that the roots are also solutions, we conclude that $f(x)\le 0$ for all $x\in [-2,\frac{1}{2}]⋃[1,\frac{4}{3}]⋃[5,\infty ).$

Let $r$ be the radius of the snowball and let $A$ be its surface area. Both $r$ and $A$ change with time. In particular, we are given that

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{5}\,\text{in/s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ when $A=100\pi \,{\text{in}}^{2}.$

To start, let's write down the formula for the surface area of a sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 8\pi r\end{aligned}
$$

We then calculate the value of $r$ using $A=100\pi .$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ 100\pi  & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ 25 & ={r}^{2} \\ r & =\pm 5\end{aligned}
$$

Since radius cannot be negative, we have $r=5.$

We now substitute $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{5}$ and $r=5$ into our expression for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{5}\cdot 8\pi \cdot 5 \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the surface area of the snowball is decreasing at a rate of $8\pi \,{\text{in}}^{2}\text{/s}.$

Consider a general vector $\,\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.$ Multiplying by the matrix $T,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T\cdot \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -2 & 7\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5y \\ -2x+7y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the linear transformation $\,T\,$ is given by

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}5y \\ -2x+7y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Here, $A$ is a $2\times 1$ matrix and $B$ is a $1\times 2$ matrix. 

There is $1$ column in $A$ and $1$ row in $B,$ so $A$ and $B$ are conformable for multiplication: 

$$
{A}_{2\times \boxed{\text{1}}}{\cdot }_{✓}{B}_{\boxed{\text{1}}\times 2}={AB}_{2\times 2}
$$

Let's compute $AB,$ one element at a time:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{bmatrix}, &  & \,5=5\cdot 1 \\  & \begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 & -15 \\ ∗ & ∗\end{bmatrix}, &  & \,-15=5\cdot (-3) \\  & \begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 & -15 \\ -2 & ∗\end{bmatrix}, &  & \,-2=-2\cdot 1 \\  & \begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 & -15 \\ -2 & 6\end{bmatrix}, &  & \,6=-2\cdot (-3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 
$AB=\begin{bmatrix}5 & -15 \\ -2 & 6\end{bmatrix}.$

Recall that given $A=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

Also, we are told that the second part of the invertible matrix theorem is true. So, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement “$A$ is invertible” is true by the first part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement $det(A)=0$ is false by the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement “$Ax=0$ has an infinite number of solutions” is false by the third part of the invertible matrix theorem.

Therefore, only statement “$A$ is invertible” is true.

To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-\frac{7}{2} & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{1}{3}(x-\frac{7}{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{1}{9}{(x-\frac{7}{2})}^{2} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+\frac{11}{4} & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{1}{3}(y+\frac{11}{4}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{1}{9}{(y+\frac{11}{4})}^{2} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{9}{(x-\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{9}{(y+\frac{11}{4})}^{2} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{1}{9}{(x-\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{9}{(y+\frac{11}{4})}^{2} & =1 \\ {(x-\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+{(y+\frac{11}{4})}^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian equation is ${(x-\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+{(y+\frac{11}{4})}^{2}=9.$

First, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{csc}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3\,\operatorname{csc}⁡x-6 & =0 \\ 3\,\operatorname{csc}⁡x & =6 \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
{x}_{1}=arcsin\,\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{\pi }{6}
$$

Our first solution lies in the $1$st quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the $2$nd quadrant, and it also has ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$

![](images/b0/b0738a8a505b89ff687cb4de350a00f2e10d6209fbeee7dcdfdf0ee359a9cc3c.png)

Since the second solution lies in the $2$nd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution for the given equation is

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{6}+2\pi n,\,x=\frac{5\pi }{6}+2\pi n.
$$

Therefore, since ${\theta }_{1}<{\theta }_{2},$ we have ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{6},\text{ }{\theta }_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6},\text{ }\text{and}\text{ }b=2\pi .$

For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,{y}_{0}=y({x}_{0}),
$$

the modified Euler method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{p}^{′})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned}
$$

where ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the initially predicted slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=-\frac{1}{2},$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=-\frac{1}{2}-(-1)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

First, we add the initial condition data to a table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $1$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Now, we compute the value of ${y}^{′}$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =1((-1)^{2}+1) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $1$ | $2$ |  |  |  |  |

Next, we compute $Δ{y}_{p}$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1$ |  |  |  |

The coordinates of the initially predicted new point given by the predictor equation are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=-1+\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}, \\ {y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p}=1+1=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add the second value to the table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ |  |  |

So, the predicted slope at this point is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ={y}_{p}\cdot (({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}+1) \\  & =2\cdot ({\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}+1) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $\frac{5}{2}$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{p}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2+\frac{5}{2})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{9}{8}$ |

The value of $x$ in the next row is ${x}_{\text{new}}=2.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $Δy$ to $y:$

$$
{y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy=1+\frac{9}{8}=\frac{17}{8}.
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{9}{8}$ |
| $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{17}{8}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)≈\frac{17}{8}.$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -6 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}.$

Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =-3$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}-3-(-3) & -6 \\ 0 & -3-(-3)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}-6{w}_{2} &=1 \\ 0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{2}=-\frac{1}{6}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{1}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{1}=0,$  we get

$$
w=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{1}{6}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-3t}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{1}{6}\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ -\frac{{c}_{2}}{6}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ -\frac{{c}_{2}}{6}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t}+\begin{bmatrix}-12 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-3t}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t}+\begin{bmatrix}-12 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-3t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(1-12t){e}^{-3t} \\ 2\,{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =5$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}5-5 & 0 \\ 4 & 5-5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2} &=0 \\ 4{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2} &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get

$$
w=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{4} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$

$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{5t}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -12\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{5t}+\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{5t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{5t}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -12\end{bmatrix}\,t{e}^{5t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3\,{e}^{5t} \\ (2-12t)\,{e}^{5t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax=b\,⟹\,\underbrace{(LU)}_{A}x=b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, setting $Ux=y,$ we obtain

$$
L\underbrace{(Ux)}_{y}=b\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}Ly &=b \\ Ux &=y.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We now solve $Ly=b.$ Writing this equation in matrix form, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This gives the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} &=3 \\ -4{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} &=-1 \\ 3{y}_{1}+2{y}_{2}+{y}_{3} &=4.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We can compute the solution to this system using forward substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =3, \\ {y}_{2} & =-1+4{y}_{1} \\  & =-1+4(3) \\  & =11, \\ {y}_{3} & =4-3{y}_{1}-2{y}_{2} \\  & =4-3(3)-2(11) \\  & =-27.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 
$y=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 11 \\ -27\end{bmatrix}.$

For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c
$$

the increment in $y$ using the Runge-Kutta (RK4) method with step size $Δx$ is computed as the weighted average of four sample slopes:

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the initial point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{1}^{′}=f({x}_{1},{y}_{1})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{2}^{′}=f({x}_{2},{y}_{2})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{3}^{′}=f({x}_{3},{y}_{3})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{3},{y}_{3})=(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx).$

Now, we have the following table of values:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-2$ | $0$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ |  |

With this in mind, let's find each point at which the slope is evaluated in turn using the values given in the table.

- The slope ${y}^{′}$ is evaluated at the initial point $(x,y)=({x}_{0},{y}_{0})=(1,-2).$

- The estimated slope ${y}_{1}^{′}$ is evaluated at

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{1},{y}_{1}) & =(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2},\,-2+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0\cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{5}{4},-2).\end{aligned}
$$

- The estimated slope ${y}_{2}^{′}$ is evaluated at

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{2},{y}_{2}) & =(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2},\,-2+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{5}{4},-\frac{7}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

- The estimated slope ${y}_{3}^{′}$ is evaluated at

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{3},{y}_{3}) & =(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(1+\frac{1}{2},\,-2+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{3}{2},-\frac{7}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, of the given options, the only point where the slope is **NOT** evaluated is $(\frac{3}{2},-2).$

the increment in $y$ using the Runge-Kutta (RK4) method with step size $Δx$ is computed as the weighted average of four sample slopes:

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the initial point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{1}^{′}=f({x}_{1},{y}_{1})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{2}^{′}=f({x}_{2},{y}_{2})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{3}^{′}=f({x}_{3},{y}_{3})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{3},{y}_{3})=(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx).$

Now, we have the following table of values:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $4$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  |

With this in mind, let's find each point at which the slope is evaluated in turn using the values given in the table.

- The slope ${y}^{′}$ is evaluated at the initial point $(x,y)=({x}_{0},{y}_{0})=(0,1).$

- The estimated slope ${y}_{1}^{′}$ is evaluated at

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{1},{y}_{1}) & =(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(0+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4},\,1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot \frac{1}{4}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{8},\frac{3}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

- The estimated slope ${y}_{2}^{′}$ is evaluated at

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{2},{y}_{2}) & =(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(0+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4},\,1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-2)\cdot \frac{1}{4}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{8},\frac{3}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

- The estimated slope ${y}_{3}^{′}$ is evaluated at

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{3},{y}_{3}) & =(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(0+\frac{1}{4},\,1+(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{4}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, of the given options, the slope is evaluated at the points $(\frac{1}{8},\frac{3}{2})$; $(\frac{1}{8},\frac{3}{4})$ only.

For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c
$$

the increment in $y$ using the Runge-Kutta (RK4) method with step size $Δx$ is computed as the weighted average of four sample slopes:

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the initial point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{1}^{′}=f({x}_{1},{y}_{1})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{2}^{′}=f({x}_{2},{y}_{2})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{3}^{′}=f({x}_{3},{y}_{3})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{3},{y}_{3})=(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx).$

All four sample slopes are already computed. So, we just need to find the increment on $y.$

We compute $Δy$ using the Runge-Kutta method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(2+2\cdot 4+2\cdot 5+9)\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot 29 \\  & =\frac{29}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the completed first row is as given below.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $2$ | $2$ | $4$ | $5$ | $9$ | $\frac{29}{6}$ |

To get the values of $x$ and $y$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x$ and $Δy$ to $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =2+\frac{29}{6} \\  & =\frac{41}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these rows to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $2$ | $2$ | $4$ | $5$ | $9$ | $\frac{29}{6}$ |
| $1$ | $\frac{41}{6}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1)≈\frac{41}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,{y}_{0}=y({x}_{0}),
$$

the Modified Euler Method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{p}^{′})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned}
$$

where ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the initially predicted slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$

First, we compute the value of ${y}^{′}$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2x+y \\  & =2\cdot 0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ |  |  |  |  |

Next, we compute $Δ{y}_{p}$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =1\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  |  |  |

The coordinates of the initially predicted new point given by the predictor equation are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=0+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}, \\ {y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p}=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add the second value to the table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ |  |  |

So, the predicted slope at this point is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =2\cdot {x}_{\text{new}}+{y}_{p} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ | $\frac{5}{2}$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{p}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1+\frac{5}{2})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{7}{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ | $\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{7}{8}$ |

The value of $x$ in the next row is ${x}_{\text{new}}=\frac{1}{2}.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $Δy$ to $y:$

$$
{y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy=1+\frac{7}{8}=\frac{15}{8}.
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ | $\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{7}{8}$ |
| $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{15}{8}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y\,\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)≈\frac{15}{8}.$

$$

For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c
$$

the increment in $y$ using the Runge-Kutta (RK4) method with step size $Δx$ is computed as the weighted average of four sample slopes:

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the initial point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{1}^{′}=f({x}_{1},{y}_{1})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{2}^{′}=f({x}_{2},{y}_{2})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{3}^{′}=f({x}_{3},{y}_{3})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{3},{y}_{3})=(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx).$

Now, we have the following table of values:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $2$ | $-2$ | $0$ | $3$ |  |

With this in mind, let's find each point at which the slope is evaluated in turn using the values given in the table.

- The slope ${y}^{′}$ is evaluated at the initial point $(x,y)=({x}_{0},{y}_{0})=(1,2).$

- The estimated slope ${y}_{1}^{′}$ is evaluated at

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{1},{y}_{1}) & =(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2},\,2+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{5}{4},\frac{5}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

- The estimated slope ${y}_{2}^{′}$ is evaluated at

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{2},{y}_{2}) & =(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2},\,2+\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-2)\cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{5}{4},\frac{3}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

- The estimated slope ${y}_{3}^{′}$ is evaluated at

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{3},{y}_{3}) & =(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(1+\frac{1}{2},\,2+0\cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{3}{2},2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, of the given options, the slope is evaluated at the points $(\frac{5}{4},\frac{5}{2})$; $(\frac{5}{4},\frac{3}{2})$; $(\frac{3}{2},2)$.

A *decoupled system* consists of equations depending on only one variable, such as

$$
{x}_{i}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{i}{x}_{i}(t),
$$

where ${\lambda }_{i}$ is a constant. This means that we can solve each equation independently. 

With this in mind, let's examine our systems.

- System $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=6{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=4{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$ is *not* decoupled because some of its equations depend on more than one variable. For example, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=6{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$

- System $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=5{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=-8{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$ is decoupled since its equations depend on only one variable each. Indeed, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=5{x}_{1}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-8{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{2}(t).$

- System $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=-{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$ is *not* decoupled because some of its equations depend on more than one variable. For example, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=5{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=-8{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$ only.

A *decoupled system* consists of equations depending on only one variable, such as

$$
{x}_{i}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{i}{x}_{i}(t),
$$

where ${\lambda }_{i}$ is a constant. This means that we can solve each equation independently. 

With this in mind, let's examine our systems.

For example, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=3{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$

- System $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=4{x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &={x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$ is *not* decoupled because some of its equations depend on more than one variable. Indeed, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-9{x}_{1}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=6{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{2}(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=-9{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=6{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$ only.

$$

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.

Now, notice that:

must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{6t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{6t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{6t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/24/2473117cdca4318187b94374820c0a12576e998e7f631a6e7bf51e56c985be43.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{6t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{4t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{6t})^{′}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}}{6{c}_{1}{e}^{6t}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}}{3{c}_{1}}{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

![](images/e8/e8110ea6d6a113e72e35502030afb495a23bc81106d64874582d03aae81b7c73.png)

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a saddle point}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ has the equation 

$$
y=x.
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on that line and approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, $y=x$ is $\text{an unstable}$ line.

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x.
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on that line and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, $y=-x$ is $\text{a stable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a saddle point}.$ 

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:

For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′} &=f(x,y,z)\, && z(a)=d,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{″}-3y{y}^{′} & =2{x}^{2} \\ x{y}^{″} & =2{x}^{2}+3y{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{2{x}^{2}+3y{y}^{′}}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{2{x}^{2}+3yz}{x}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is
$z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=1.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(1)=-1, \\ {z}^{′} &=\frac{2{x}^{2}+3yz}{x},\, && z(1)=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

Since we want to find the values of $y$ and ${y}^{′}=z$ at $x=\frac{3}{2},$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=\frac{3}{2}-1=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

First, we place the initial condition data in the table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ |  |  | $1$ |  |  |

Next, we compute both ${y}^{′}$ and ${z}^{′}$ according to the given rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=1 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{2{x}^{2}+3yz}{x} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot {1}^{2}+3\cdot (-1)\cdot 1}{1} \\  & =\frac{2-3}{1} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $1$ |  | $1$ | $-1$ |  |

Next, we compute $Δy$ and $Δz$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =1\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ |

To get the new values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x,$ $Δy$ to $y,$ and $Δz$ to $z,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=-1+\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{1}{2} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=1+\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these values to our table in a new row gives the following:

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ |  |  | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)≈-\frac{1}{2}$
and
${y}^{′}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)=z\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)≈\frac{1}{2}.$

Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+y &=0 \\ 4x+2y &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Notice that the second equation is a multiple of the first one:

$$
2(2x+y)=4x+2y,
$$

so we can disregard the second equation.

From the first equation, we get

$$
2x+y=0\,⇒\,y=-2x.
$$

Therefore, the equilibrium points are given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}k \\ -2k\end{bmatrix},\,k\in R.
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 6 \\ -3 & 3\end{bmatrix}.$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3\text{i}t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}+\text{i}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$

A numerical method  ${y}_{n+1}={y}_{n}+Δ{y}_{n}$ is stable for a given step size $Δx$ if, when applied to the test equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-\lambda y,\,y(0)=\frac{1}{2},\,x\ge 0,\,\lambda >0,
$$

the numerical solution satisfies ${y}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty ,$ just like the exact solution.

When a method is applied to the test equation, the update takes the form

$$
{y}_{n+1}=R(\lambda Δx){y}_{n},
$$

where $R(\lambda Δx)$ is the stability function of the method. The set of values for which the method is stable, given by $|R(\lambda Δx)|<1,$ is called the stability region of the method.

A method that is stable for all possible values $\lambda Δx>0$ is called absolutely stable.

Now, let’s check the stability of the modified Euler Method by applying it to the test equation  

$$
{y}^{′}=-2y,\,y(0)=1.
$$

We now examine our statements:

- Applying the modified Euler method to this test equation, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{n}+Δ{y}_{n}^{(p)} & ={y}_{n}+f({x}_{n},{y}_{n})\cdot Δx \\  & ={y}_{n}-2{y}_{n}\cdot Δx\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{n+1} & ={y}_{n}+\frac{1}{2}(f({x}_{n},{y}_{n})+f({x}_{n+1},{y}_{n}-2{y}_{n}\cdot Δx))\cdot Δx \\  & ={y}_{n}+\frac{1}{2}(-2{y}_{n}-2({y}_{n}-2{y}_{n}\cdot Δx))\cdot Δx \\  & ={y}_{n}+\frac{1}{2}(-4{y}_{n}+4{y}_{n}\cdot Δx)\cdot Δx \\  & ={y}_{n}-2{y}_{n}\cdot Δx+2{y}_{n}\cdot (Δx)^{2} \\  & =[1-2Δx+2(Δx)^{2}]{y}_{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the stability function is $R(2Δx)=1-2Δx+2(Δx)^{2}.$ Hence, statement “The stability function is $R(2Δx)=1-2Δx+2(Δx)^{2}.$” is true.

- The method is stable when

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(2Δx)| & <1 \\ |1-2Δx+2(Δx)^{2}| & <1 \\ |2{(Δx-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}| & <1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${y}_{n}$ converges to $0$ as $n\to \infty $ if and only if

$$
|2{(Δx-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}|<1.
$$

Hence, statement “The stability region is $|2{(Δx-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}|<1.$” is true.

- Now, since the argument of the absolute value is always non-negative, we can remove the absolute value. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(Δx-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} & <1 \\ 2{(Δx-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & <\frac{1}{2} \\ {(Δx-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & <\frac{1}{4} \\ -\frac{1}{2}<Δx-\frac{1}{2} & <\frac{1}{2} \\ 0<Δx & <1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the modified Euler method is not absolutely stable, and statement “The method is absolutely stable” is false.

- Finally, since it satisfies this inequality, the modified Euler method is stable for step size $Δx=\frac{1}{2},$ and hence statement “The method is stable for step size $Δx=\frac{1}{2}.$” is true.

In conclusion, the correct answer is “The stability function is $R(2Δx)=1-2Δx+2(Δx)^{2}.$”; “The stability region is $|2{(Δx-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}|<1.$”; “The method is stable for step size $Δx=\frac{1}{2}.$” only.

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4+6\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4+6\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{(4+6\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{(4+6\text{i})t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{4t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+2\text{i}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-2{e}^{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {e}^{4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t))+\text{i}{e}^{4t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)) \\ {e}^{4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{4t}+\text{i}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t).$

$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{(-4+\text{i})t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t}+\text{i}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}

The Wronskian $W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})$ of two vector-valued functions 

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{11}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t)\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{22}(t)\end{bmatrix}
$$

is defined as

$$
W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=det({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=\begin{vmatrix}{x}_{11}(t) & {x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t) & {x}_{22}(t)\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Note the following:

- If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

- If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly dependent.

First, we write our system in matrix form:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

Now, let's substitute the given vectors into the matrix differential equation:

- $a(t)=\begin{bmatrix}4{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}(4{e}^{2t})^{′} \\ (0)^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}8{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 4{e}^{2t}+1\cdot 0 \\ 0\cdot 4{e}^{2t}+3\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}8{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}8{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $b(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{3t} \\ 2{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}(2{e}^{3t})^{′} \\ (2{e}^{3t})^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{3t} \\ 2{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}6{e}^{3t} \\ 6{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 2{e}^{3t}+1\cdot 2{e}^{3t} \\ 0\cdot 2{e}^{3t}+3\cdot 2{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}6{e}^{3t} \\ 6{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}6{e}^{3t} \\ 6{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $c(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{isn't}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}({e}^{2t})^{′} \\ ({e}^{2t})^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot {e}^{2t}+1\cdot {e}^{2t} \\ 0\cdot {e}^{2t}+3\cdot {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{2t} \\ 3{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the set of solutions ${a,b}.$ Its Wronskian is

$$
\begin{aligned}W(a,b) & =\begin{vmatrix}4{e}^{2t} & 2{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{3t}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(4{e}^{2t})\cdot 2{e}^{3t}-(2{e}^{3t})\cdot 0 \\  & =8{e}^{5t}-0 \\  & =8{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

which is nonzero for at least one $t\in R.$ Thus, since $a$ and $b$ are both solutions of the same linear system, and their Wronskian is nonzero for at least one $t\in R,$ ${a,b}$ is a set of fundamental solutions of the system.

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{11}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t)\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{22}(t)\end{bmatrix}
$$

is defined as

$$
W({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=det({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=\begin{vmatrix}{x}_{11}(t) & {x}_{12}(t) \\ {x}_{21}(t) & {x}_{22}(t)\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Note the following:

- If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

- If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are linearly dependent. In this case, they do **not** form a fundamental set of solutions.

First, we write our system in matrix form:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -3 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}x(t).
$$

Now, let's substitute the given vectors into the matrix differential equation:

- $a(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1-3t \\ 3t\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}(1-3t)^{′} \\ (3t)^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -3 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1-3t \\ 3t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3(1-3t)+(-3)\cdot 3t \\ 3(1-3t)+3\cdot 3t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $b(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2(1-3t) \\ 6t\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{is}$ also a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}(2(1-3t))^{′} \\ (6t)^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -3 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2(1-3t) \\ 6t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3\cdot 2(1-3t)+(-3)\cdot 6t \\ 3\cdot 2(1-3t)+3\cdot 6t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $c(t)=\begin{bmatrix}t \\ t\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{isn't}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}(t)^{′} \\ (t)^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -3 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}t \\ t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3t+(-3)t \\ 3t+3t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-6t \\ 6t\end{bmatrix}\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the set of solutions ${a,b}.$ Its Wronskian is

$$
\begin{aligned}W(a,b) & =\begin{vmatrix}1-3t & 2(1-3t) \\ 3t & 6t\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1-3t)\cdot 6t-2(1-3t)\cdot 3t \\  & =6t(1-3t)-6t(1-3t) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which is zero for all $t\in R.$ Thus, since $a$ and $b$ are both solutions of the same linear system, but their Wronskian is identically zero, they are linearly dependent and do **not** form a fundamental set of solutions of the system.
