Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =0,\,v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix},\,w=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix} & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}) \\  & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}t-\frac{1}{3} \\ 3t\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that ${x}_{E}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}$ are equilibrium solutions of the system since ${x}_{E}^{′}(t)=0.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=3x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

![](images/3a/3a70188cf5de7e7b64530aa661447b7fa7fc1e918ca3de41088e67274d813b7a.png)

Now, we consider some general solutions of the form 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}t-\frac{1}{3} \\ 3t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

For example:

- When ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=3,$ we get the following curve: 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=3t \\ y &=9t+3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Let's add it to the phase space:

![](images/37/37deb5a0fda7ef15a016ec2d73a3b935074b6696184dd480ebe5b858ce517500.png)

- When ${c}_{1}=-1$ and ${c}_{2}=-3,$ we get the following curve: 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-3t \\ y &=-9t-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Let's add it to the phase space:

![](images/60/60b49680cf94888122f25432586a3546dea206ae960f951afd187444afc8881a.png)

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](images/7b/7b4de40b147f1745986476ab0b0cbad22ad0484924f62389c6c19187d5d06245.png)

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} & t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} & t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{3(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{3(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$

$$

Therefore, we get

$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x(0) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1-{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1-{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1-{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

To shift the system's equilibrium from ${x}^{∗}$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗},
$$

where $u=\begin{bmatrix}u(t) \\ v(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

In our case, we have

$$
u=x-\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\,⇒\,x=u+\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}={u}^{′}.
$$

Substituting $x$ and ${x}^{′}$ into the given system, we obtain

$$

$$

$$

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),

$$

Euler's method approximates the solution of an initial value problem containing a system of ODEs by applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

First, because the initial conditions are $y(0)=0,$ $z(0)=1,$ and $w(0)=1,$ we place $y=0,$ $z=1,$ and $w=1$ in the table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ | $w$ | ${w}^{′}$ | $Δw$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ |  |  | $1$ |  |  | $1$ |  |  |

Next, we compute ${y}^{′},{z}^{′},$ and ${w}^{′}$ according to the given rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =1+x-2y+3z \\  & =1+0-2\cdot 0+3\cdot 1 \\  & =4 \\ {z}^{′} & =2y-w \\  & =2\cdot 0-1 \\  & =-1 \\ {w}^{′} & =-x+yz \\  & =-0+0\cdot 1 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ | $w$ | ${w}^{′}$ | $Δw$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $4$ |  | $1$ | $-1$ |  | $1$ | $0$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy,$ $Δz,$ and $Δw$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =1 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4} \\ Δw & ={w}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =0\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ | $w$ | ${w}^{′}$ | $Δw$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $4$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{1}{4}$ | $1$ | $0$ | $0$ |

To get the new values of $x,$ $y,$ $z,$ and $w$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x,$ $Δy$ to $y,$ $Δz$ to $z,$ and $Δw$ to $w,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=0+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{4} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=0+1=1 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=1+\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)=\frac{3}{4} \\ {w}_{\text{new}} & =w+Δw=1+0=1\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these values to our table in a new row gives the following:

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ | $w$ | ${w}^{′}$ | $Δw$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $4$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{1}{4}$ | $1$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $\frac{1}{4}$ | $1$ |  |  | $\frac{3}{4}$ |  |  | $1$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y\,\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)≈1,$
$z\,\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)≈\frac{3}{4},$
and
$w\,\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)≈1.$

$$
u=x-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\,⇒\,x=u+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}={u}^{′}.
$$

In coordinate form, this can be written as follows:

$$

The diagram shows a series RL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $10\,Ω,$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RL circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=10\,Ω.$

$$
{V}_{R}=10I
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$

$$
{V}_{L}=2\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ in the circuit is

$$
6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)=10I+2\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+5I=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+5{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-5t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))+5(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ (-2\alpha +5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+(5\alpha +2\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2\alpha +5\beta &=3\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ 5\alpha +2\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{6}{29},$ $\beta =\frac{15}{29}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{6}{29}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{15}{29}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-5t}-\frac{6}{29}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{15}{29}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-5t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{6}{29}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{15}{29}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{6}{29}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{15}{29}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(-\frac{6}{29}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{15}{29}\right)}^{2}}≈0.56\,\text{A},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

$$

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-16\lambda m+64{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-8\lambda )(m-8\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=8\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{8\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{8\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{8\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{8\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =8A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda x}+B{e}^{8\lambda x}+8B\lambda x{e}^{8\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}8A\lambda +B & =0 \\ (8\lambda )A+B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+2(8A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+8B\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+B+2(8A\lambda +B+8B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+B+16A\lambda +2B+16B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+16\lambda )A+(3+16\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(8\lambda )A+B &=0 \\ (1+16\lambda )A+(3+16\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}8\lambda  & 1 \\ 1+16\lambda  & 3+16\lambda \end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$

For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

First, since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=\frac{1}{3},$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=\frac{1}{3}-0=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3x+2y+(3{x}_{\text{new}}+2{y}_{\text{new}}))\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(3x+2y+3{x}_{\text{new}}+2{y}_{\text{new}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(3x+2y+3{x}_{\text{new}})+\frac{1}{3}{y}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{6}(3x+2y+3{x}_{\text{new}})+\frac{1}{3}{y}_{\text{new}} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{6}(3x+3{x}_{\text{new}}+8y)+\frac{1}{3}{y}_{\text{new}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve for the general formula for ${y}_{\text{new}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{6}(3x+3{x}_{\text{new}}+8y) \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{4}(3x+3{x}_{\text{new}}+8y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is ${x}_{\text{new}}=0+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}.$ Hence, the new $y$ value is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{4}(3x+3{x}_{\text{new}}+8y) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(3\cdot 0+3\cdot \frac{1}{3}+8\cdot 0) \\  & =\frac{1}{4} \\  & =0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y\,\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)≈0.25.$

- ${y}_{3}^{′}=f({x}_{3},{y}_{3})$ is the slope at $({x}_{3},{y}_{3})=(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx).$

$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

First, since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=0,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=0-\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y(2{x}^{3}+3)+{y}_{\text{new}}(2({x}_{\text{new}})^{3}+3))\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}y(2{x}^{3}+3)+\frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}(2({x}_{\text{new}})^{3}+3).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{4}y(2{x}^{3}+3)+\frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}(2({x}_{\text{new}})^{3}+3) \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{4}y(2{x}^{3}+7)+\frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}(2({x}_{\text{new}})^{3}+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve for the general formula for ${y}_{\text{new}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}}-\frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}(2({x}_{\text{new}})^{3}+3) & =\frac{1}{4}y(2{x}^{3}+7) \\ \frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}(1-2({x}_{\text{new}})^{3}) & =\frac{1}{4}y(2{x}^{3}+7) \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{y(2{x}^{3}+7)}{1-2({x}_{\text{new}})^{3}}\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(0)≈2.25.$

We model the price growth using the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}t}=0.042P.
$$

The solution to this equation is

$$
P(t)={P}_{0}\,{e}^{0.042t},
$$

where ${P}_{0}$ is the initial value.

We're told that the price today is $$120,$ so we have ${P}_{0}=120.$

Therefore, the price $P$ of the product after $t$ years is

$$
P(t)=120\,{e}^{0.042t}\,.
$$

To find how many years it takes for the price to grow to $$750,$ we substitute $P(t)=750$ into the equation above and solve for $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}750 & =120\,{e}^{0.042t} \\ \frac{750}{120} & ={e}^{0.042t} \\ {e}^{0.042t} & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{0.042t}) & =ln\,\left(\frac{25}{4}\right) \\ 0.042t & =ln\,\left(\frac{25}{4}\right) \\ t & =\frac{1}{0.042}ln\,\left(\frac{25}{4}\right) \\ t & ≈43.633\end{aligned}
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we conclude that it takes $44$ years for the price to increase to $$750.$

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

- The function $f(x)$ is piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,\infty ).$ The function has jump discontinuities at $x=0,1,2,…,$ and any closed interval $[a,b]⊂[0,\infty )$ will contain finitely many discontinuities.

To find the function $g(t),$ we need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of the term containing the time delay in $Y(s).$

We focus on the term with the exponential ${e}^{-\pi s/2}$ (which corresponds to the step function in the time domain) and identify the rational function part:

$$
F(s)=\frac{s}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+2)}.
$$

We'll solve this in three steps.

**Step 1.** Partial fraction decomposition

Since the denominator contains a linear factor $(s+2)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+4),$ the decomposition takes the form

$$
\frac{s}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+2)}=\frac{A}{s+2}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+4}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
s=A({s}^{2}+4)+(Bs+C)(s+2).
$$

Now, we find the constants $A,B,$ and $C.$

- Setting $s=-2,$ we have

$$
-2=A((-2)^{2}+4)+0\,⟹\,8A=-2\,⟹\,A=-\frac{1}{4}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have

$$
0=A+B\,⟹\,B=-A=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have

$$
0=4A+2C\,⟹\,0=4\,\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)+2C\,⟹\,C=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Thus, we can rewrite $F(s)$ as

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{4}(-\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}).
$$

**Step 2.** Finding the Inverse of the base function

We find the inverse transform $f(t)={L}^{-1}{F(s)}$ using standard transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{1}{4}(-{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+2}}+{L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}}+{L}^{-1}{\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-{e}^{-2t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Applying the time-shifting property

Finally, we address the ${e}^{-\pi s/2}$ term. By the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
{e}^{-as}\cdot F(s)=L{u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a)}.
$$

Taking the inverse Laplace transform gives

$$
{L}^{-1}{{e}^{-as}F(s)}=u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a).
$$

In our case, $a=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Therefore, we shift $f(t)$ by replacing every instance of $t$ with $(t-\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})f\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot \frac{1}{4}[-{e}^{-2(t-\pi /2)}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))].\end{aligned}
$$

Using the trigonometric identities $cos\,(2\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$ and $sin\,(2\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),$ we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot \frac{1}{4}(-{e}^{-2(t-\pi /2)}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\,u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})({e}^{-2(t-\pi /2)}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing this to the second term of the form given in the problem statement $y(t)=-2{e}^{-2t}-\frac{1}{4}u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot g(t),$ we identify $g(t)$ as

$$
g(t)={e}^{-2(t-\pi /2)}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

- The set $B$ is a subspace. It represents a line, and a line is a subspace if and only if it passes through the origin. Here, the components of the zero vector $0=⟨0,0⟩$ satisfy the equation $x=2y$ since $0=2\cdot 0.$ So, $0$ lies in $B.$

- The set $C$ is a subspace. It also represents a line, and a line is a subspace if and only if it passes through the origin. Here, the components of the zero vector $0=⟨0,0⟩$ satisfy the equation $x-y=0$ since $0-0=0.$ So, $0$ lies in $C.$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-20x & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{2}-20x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(20x) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(20x) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2y)-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 20 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{3}{10},$ $x=5,$ and $y=10,$ and solving for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2y)-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 20 & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2\cdot 10)-\left(\frac{3}{10}\right)\cdot 20 & =0 \\ 20\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-6 & =0 \\ 20\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =6 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

$\omega =2.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+ϕ)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =2$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[4(D-Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4(C+Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)]+4t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ 4D\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4C\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Only solutions $y$ $=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+ϕ)$ $-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$ $+\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ and $y$ $=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+ϕ)$ $-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$ $+\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ match the forms above.

We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right))+x(-\frac{\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)+\frac{\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right):$

$$
[-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\pi A &=0 \\ \pi B &=6\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=0 \\ B &=\frac{6}{\pi }\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\frac{6x}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

We need to solve the equation $Ax=0.$ First, we find the row echelon form of $A$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 2 & 5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

This corresponds to the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=0 \\ {x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The second equation tells us that ${x}_{2}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get 

$$
{x}_{1}+2(0)=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=0.
$$

So, we conclude that $x=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ is the only solution to this system.

Therefore, $\text{Null}(A)=\{0\}.$

First, we notice that the domain of the function is $x\in (-1,\infty ).$

A function $f(x)$ is concave down on an interval $(a,b)$ if ${f}^{″}(x)<0$ for all $x\in (a,b).$

First, let's calculate the second derivative of $f(x)=6x+\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+4)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =6+\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{1}{x+4} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(x+4)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find where the function is concave down, we solve the inequality ${f}^{″}(x)<0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(x+4)^{2}} & <0 \\ \frac{1}{(x+4)^{2}} & <\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that for $x>-1$ we have $(x+1)^{2}<(x+4)^{2},$ and thus $\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}>\frac{1}{(x+4)^{2}}.$ 

Therefore, $\frac{1}{(x+4)^{2}}<\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}$ is always true in the given domain, and we conclude that the largest interval where $f(x)$ is concave down is $(\,-1,\infty \,).$

Let $r$ be the radius, $A$ the area, and $C$ the circumference of the circle. We wish to find $D$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=9\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {\left(\frac{C}{2\pi }\right)}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}\left(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=9\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}9\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi } \\ 9 & =\frac{C}{2\pi } \\ C & =18\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $C=2\pi r,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi r & =18\pi  \\ r & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $D=2r,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =2\cdot 9 \\ D & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the given expression for $q(t),$ we obtain the following expression for $I,$ in amperes:

$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=-2{e}^{-2t}+15{e}^{-5t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{8}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

$$

$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(-\frac{6}{5}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{8}{5}\right)}^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{36+64}{25}}=2.
$$

The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $(10\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $15\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.1\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $5\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=15\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=15I=15\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.1}=10q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=5\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=5\,\frac{dI}{dt}=5\,\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dq}{dt}\right)=5\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
10\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)=15\,\frac{dq}{dt}+10q+5\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}},
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{dq}{dt}+2q=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+2{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-2t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a sinusoidal with argument $t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t))+3(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t))\, &  \\ +2(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ (-3\alpha +\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+(\alpha +3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3\alpha +\beta &=2\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) \\ \alpha +3\beta &=-1\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{7}{10},$ $\beta =-\frac{1}{10}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{7}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-2t}-\frac{7}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-2t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{7}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
q(t)≈{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{7}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=30\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=30I=30\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.05}=20q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=5\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=5\,\frac{dI}{dt}=5\,\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dq}{dt}\right)=5\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
8\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-41\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=30\,\frac{dq}{dt}+20q+5\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}},
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+6\cdot \frac{dq}{dt}+4q=\frac{8}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{41}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

$$

$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$

$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $3t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a sinusoidal with argument $3t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+6(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\, &  \\ +4(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{8}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{41}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ (-5\alpha +18\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+(-18\alpha -5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =\frac{8}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{41}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$

$$

$$

To apply the ratio test, we define ${a}_{n}=\frac{{x}^{n}}{{4}^{n}(5n-2)}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{x}^{n+1}}{{4}^{n+1}(5n+3)}\cdot \frac{{4}^{n}(5n-2)}{{x}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{x(5n-2)}{4(5n+3)}| \\  & =\frac{|x|}{4}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{5n-2}{5n+3} \\  & =\frac{|x|}{4}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{|x|}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{|x|}{4}<1\,⟹\,|x|<4.
$$

So, the radius of convergence is $4,$ and the series converges for any $x$ that lies in the open interval $(-4,4).$

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series when $L=1.$ So, when $|x|=4,$ we do not know if the series converges. This means that the endpoints $x=-4$ and $x=4$ need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

- When $x=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{{4}^{n}(5n-2)} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{4}^{n}}{{4}^{n}(5n-2)} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{5n-2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{13}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

To see if this series converges, we use the limit comparison test, with ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{5n-2}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{1}{n}.$ We observe that ${a}_{n}$ and ${b}_{n}$ are positive, and

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{{a}_{n}}{{b}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\left(\frac{1}{5n-2}\right)}{\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{n}{5n-2}=\frac{1}{5},
$$

 
which is positive and finite. Hence, the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ and ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ either *both* converge or *both* diverge.
Since ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{n}$ is divergent, the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{5n-2}$ is also divergent by the limit comparison test. So, the endpoint $x=4$ is not included in our interval.

- When $x=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{{4}^{n}(5n-2)} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-4)^{n}}{{4}^{n}(5n-2)} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{5n-2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{8}-\frac{1}{13}+⋯,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the alternating series test. So, the endpoint $x=-4$ is included in our interval.

Therefore, the interval of convergence is $[-4,4),$ or equivalently, $-4\le x<4.$

The dimension of the null space of a matrix is the number of non-pivot columns in the matrix. 

Also, all of the given matrices are in row echelon form.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the statements.

- Statement “If $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ then $\text{dim(Null}(A))=1.$” is true. The matrix $A$ has $1$ pivot column and $1$ non-pivot column. So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(A))=1.
$$

- Statement “If $B=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ then $\text{dim(Null}(B))=2.$” is true. The matrix $B$ has $1$ pivot column and $2$ non-pivot columns (namely, the $2$nd and $3$rd columns). So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(B))=2.
$$

- Statement “If $C=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ then $\text{dim(Null}(C))=3.$” is false. The matrix $C$ has $3$ pivot columns and no non-pivot columns. So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(C))=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “If $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ then $\text{dim(Null}(A))=1.$”; “If $B=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ then $\text{dim(Null}(B))=2.$” only.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{6n}}{{9}^{kn}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{\left(\frac{{3}^{6}}{{9}^{k}}\right)}^{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{\left(\frac{{9}^{3}}{{9}^{k}}\right)}^{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{({9}^{3-k})}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

We see that this is a geometric series with a common ratio of $r={9}^{3-k}.$ 

For the series to converge, we require $|r|<1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|{9}^{3-k}| & <1 \\ {9}^{3-k} & <1.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we could remove the absolute value bars because ${9}^{3-k}$ is always positive.

The equation ${9}^{3-k}=1$ has the solution $k=3.$ Now, since ${9}^{3-k}$ decreases as $k$ increases, the solution to ${9}^{3-k}<1$ must be $k>3.$

First, note that we are given $y(0)$ and asked to find $y\,\left(\frac{3}{2}\right).$ The distance from $x=0$ to $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is $\frac{3}{2},$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{(\frac{3}{2}-0)}{2}=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

Now, let's proceed with Euler's method. We'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(0)=1.$ 

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $$ | $$ |

**Step 1.** We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy$ (using the values of $x$ and $y$ in the first row) and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}}$ and ${y}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2x+2=2\cdot 0+2=2 \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=2\cdot \frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=0+\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{4} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =1+Δy=1+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{4}$ | $\frac{5}{2}$ | $$ | $$ |

 

**Step 2.** We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy$ (using the values of $x$ and $y$ in the second row) and new values of ${x}_{\text{new}}$ and ${y}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2x+2=2\cdot \frac{3}{4}+2=\frac{7}{2} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{7}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{4}=\frac{21}{8} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=\frac{3}{4}+\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{21}{8}=\frac{41}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{4}$ | $\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{7}{2}$ | $\frac{21}{8}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $\frac{41}{8}$ | $$ | $$ |

 

Therefore, we conclude that  $y\,\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)≈\frac{41}{8}.$

We need to find ${x}_{1}$,  ${x}_{2}$, and ${x}_{3}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =x \\ {x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -3 \\ 6 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 0 \\ 10 \\ 10\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ -5 \\ 16 \\ 10\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

From this, we get the system with the augmented matrix $M$, which we reduce using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & \begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 & 0 & 10 \\ -3 & 0 & 0 & -5 \\ 6 & 10 & -2 & 16 \\ 0 & 10 & 0 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ ∼ & \begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 & 0 & 10 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 5 \\ 6 & 10 & -2 & 16 \\ 0 & 10 & 0 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ ∼ & \begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 & 0 & 10 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 10 & 0 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{4} & :={R}_{4}+(-2){R}_{2} \\ ∼ & \begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 & 0 & 10 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

   

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2} &=10 \\ 5{x}_{2} &=5 \\ -2{x}_{3} &=-4 \\ 0 &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the fourth equation, we get a true statement. Then, from the second and third equation, we get ${x}_{2}=1$ and  ${x}_{3}=2$ respectively. Substituting ${x}_{2}=1$ into the first equation, we get 

$$
3{x}_{1}+5(1)=10\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{5}{3}.
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{B}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{3} \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, ${x}_{1}=\frac{5}{3}.$

We start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 5 \\ -4 & 6 & -10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to basis vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the reduced matrix has $1$ pivot column (or alternatively, it has exactly $1$ non-zero row). 

Therefore,

To apply the ratio test we define ${a}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n+1}(2x)^{n}}{(n+4)^{3/2}}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(-1)^{n+2}(2x)^{n+1}}{(n+5)^{3/2}}\cdot \frac{(n+4)^{3/2}}{(-1)^{n+1}(2x)^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{-2x(n+4)^{3/2}}{(n+5)^{3/2}}| \\  & =2|x|\cdot {lim}_{n\to \infty }{\left(\frac{n+4}{n+5}\right)}^{3/2} \\  & =2|x|\cdot 1 \\  & =2|x|\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for $2|x|<1,$ or equivalently $|x|<\frac{1}{2}.$ So, the radius of convergence is $\frac{1}{2},$ and the series converges for any $x$ that lies in the open interval $(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series when $L=1.$ So, when $|x|=\frac{1}{2},$ we do not know if the series converges. This means that the endpoints $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $x=\frac{1}{2}$ need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

- When $x=\frac{1}{2}$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}(2x)^{n}}{(n+4)^{3/2}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}\cdot (1)^{n}}{(n+4)^{3/2}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{(n+4)^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{5}^{3/2}}-\frac{1}{{6}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{7}^{3/2}}-\frac{1}{{8}^{3/2}}+⋯\,,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the alternating series test.  So the endpoint $x=\frac{1}{2}$ is included in our interval.

- When $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}(2x)^{n}}{(n+4)^{3/2}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}(-1)^{n}}{(n+4)^{3/2}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{2n+1}}{(n+4)^{3/2}} \\  & =-(\frac{1}{{5}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{6}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{7}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{8}^{3/2}}+⋯)\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We notice that each term of this series ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{(n+4)^{3/2}}$ is smaller than ${b}_{n}=\frac{1}{{n}^{3/2}}:$

$$
\frac{1}{(n+4)^{3/2}}\le \frac{1}{{n}^{3/2}}
$$

Since ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{3/2}}$ is convergent, the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(n+4)^{3/2}}$ is convergent by the comparison test. So the endpoint $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ is included in our interval.

Therefore, the interval of convergence is $[-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}],$ or equivalently, $-\frac{1}{2}\le x\le \frac{1}{2}.$

We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \,\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-\frac{1}{x}+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the exponential function to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{-1/x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{-1/x+C}\, \\ |y| & ={e}^{-1/x}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ y & =K{e}^{-1/x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the condition $y(1)=e$ to find $K:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}e & =K{e}^{-1} \\ K & ={e}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}=0$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=e$ is

$$
y={e}^{2-1/x}\,.
$$

v:
Recall that given $A=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement $det(A)=0$ is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =3\cdot (-2)-2\cdot 0 \\  & =-6\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement “$Ax=0$ has the unique  solution $⟨0,0⟩$” is true by the third part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement “$⟨5,-4⟩$ is a solution to $Ax=0$” is false. Again,  according to the third part of the invertible matrix theorem, the system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

Therefore, only statement “$Ax=0$ has the unique  solution $⟨0,0⟩$” is true.

To apply the ratio test we define ${a}_{n}=\frac{{4}^{n}{x}^{n}}{{n}^{2}+4n}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{4}^{n+1}{x}^{n+1}}{(n+1)^{2}+4(n+1)}\cdot \frac{{n}^{2}+4n}{{4}^{n}{x}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{4x({n}^{2}+4n)}{{n}^{2}+6n+5}| \\  & =|4x|\cdot {lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{{n}^{2}+4n}{{n}^{2}+6n+5} \\  & =|4x|\cdot 1 \\  & =|4x|\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for $|4x|<1,$ which means $|x|<\frac{1}{4}.$ So, the radius of convergence is $\frac{1}{4},$ and the series converges for any $x$ that lies in the open interval $(-\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{4}).$

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series when $L=1.$ So, when $|x|=\frac{1}{4},$ we do not know if the series converges. This means that the endpoints $x=-\frac{1}{4}$ and $x=\frac{1}{4}$ need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

- When $x=\frac{1}{4}$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{4}^{n}{x}^{n}}{{n}^{2}+4n} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{4}^{n}{(1/4)}^{n}}{{n}^{2}+4n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}+4n} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 5}+\frac{1}{2\cdot 6}+\frac{1}{3\cdot 7}+\frac{1}{4\cdot 8}+⋯,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the direct comparison test with the convergent $p$-series $\sum \frac{1}{{n}^{2}}.$ So the endpoint $x=\frac{1}{4}$ is included in our interval.

- When $x=-\frac{1}{4}$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{4}^{n}{x}^{n}}{{n}^{2}+4n} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{4}^{n}{(-1/4)}^{n}}{{n}^{2}+4n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}+4n} \\  & =-\frac{1}{1\cdot 5}+\frac{1}{2\cdot 6}-\frac{1}{3\cdot 7}+\frac{1}{4\cdot 8}-⋯,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the alternating series test. So the endpoint $x=-\frac{1}{4}$ is included in our interval.

Therefore, the interval of convergence is $[-\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{4}],$ or equivalently, $-\frac{1}{4}\le x\le \frac{1}{4}.$

Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement “$v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $2.$” is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =2v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=2v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =2.$

- Statement “If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2,$ then $-v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$” is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(-v)=-Av=-(2v)=2(-v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(-v)=2(-v),$ and $-v\ne 0,$ this implies that $-v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =2$ (but not $-2$).

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

$$

$$

Since $Av=6v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =6.$

- Statement “$v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $4.$” is true. We have

$$

Since $Av=4v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =4.$

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 0 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Notice that its augmented matrix $M$ is already in row echelon form:

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

 

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=\frac{3}{2}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get

$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}6{x}_{3} \\ \frac{3}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}-{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}+4y & 4x-2y\end{bmatrix},$ we must have 

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}+4y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=4x-2y.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}+4y)=-3{x}^{2}+4x \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x-2y)=-2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-2y)=4\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3{x}^{2}+4x & 4 \\ 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(4,8),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(4,8)=\begin{bmatrix}-32 & 4 \\ 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement $H(4,8)>0$ is true. Indeed, computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(4,8),$ we get

$$
H(4,8)=det({f}^{″}(4,8))=(-32)\cdot (-2)-{4}^{2}=48>0.
$$

- Statement $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(4,8)>0$ is false. We have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(4,8)=({f}^{″}(4,8))_{11}=-32<0.$

- Statement “The point $(4,8)$ is a saddle point of $f$” is false. Since $H(4,8)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(4,8)<0,$ the point $(4,8)$ is a local maximum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is $H(4,8)>0$ only.

$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{3}-6) \\  & =8xy+{y}^{3} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{3}-6) \\  & =4{x}^{2}+3x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨8xy+{y}^{3},\,4{x}^{2}+3x{y}^{2},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} &=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}8xy+{y}^{3} &=0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+3x{y}^{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $y=0$ or ${y}^{2}+8x=0.$ So, we have two cases.

- If $y=0$, substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
4{x}^{2}+3x(0)^{2}=0\,⟹\,x=0.
$$

- If ${y}^{2}=-8x$, substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
4{x}^{2}+3x(-8x)^{2}=0\,⟹\,x=0.
$$

Substituting $x=0$ back into ${y}^{2}=-8x$ gives

$$
{y}^{2}=-8(0)\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

So, in both cases, we have $x=0$ and $y=0.$ Finally, substituting these values into our function, we get

$$
z=4(0)^{2}(0)+(0)(0)^{3}-6=-6.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,-6).$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =\sqrt{3}\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -4 & -1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1-\sqrt{3}\text{i} & 1 \\ -4 & -1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+(-1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-\sqrt{3}\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ -(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}}{-1}=\sqrt{3}\text{i}-1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{3}+2x+1}{{x}^{2}-x-12} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{12}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{(x+\frac{2}{x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(1-\frac{1}{x}-\frac{12}{{x}^{2}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{2}{x},\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\frac{1}{x}$ and $\frac{12}{{x}^{2}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$

$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y=f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

First, we rewrite the series so that it's in the form ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }a{r}^{n},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{16}^{kn+1}}{{4}^{n-1}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{16}^{kn}\cdot 16}{{4}^{n}\cdot {4}^{-1}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(16\cdot 4){\left(\frac{{16}^{k}}{4}\right)}^{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }64{\left(\frac{{16}^{k}}{4}\right)}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that this is a geometric series with a common ratio of $r=\frac{{16}^{k}}{4}.$ 

For the series to converge, we require $|r|<1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\frac{{16}^{k}}{4}| & <1 \\ \frac{{16}^{k}}{4} & <1 \\ {16}^{k} & <4.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we could remove the absolute value bars because $\frac{{16}^{k}}{4}$ is always positive.

The equation ${16}^{k}=4$ has the solution $k=\frac{1}{2}.$ Now, since ${16}^{k}$ increases as $k$ increases, the solution to ${16}^{k}<4$ must be $k<\frac{1}{2}.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{(-3)\cdot 1+3\cdot (-1)+(-3)\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

The determinant of the coefficient matrix is

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =|\begin{aligned}9 & 11 \\ 6 & -k\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $x$ is given by $x=\frac{{D}_{x}}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x} & =|\begin{aligned}-14 & 11 \\ -34 & -k\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{D}_{x}}{D} \\ -4 & =\frac{|\begin{aligned}-14 & 11 \\ -34 & -k\end{aligned}|}{|\begin{aligned}9 & 11 \\ 6 & -k\end{aligned}|} \\ -4|\begin{aligned}9 & 11 \\ 6 & -k\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}-14 & 11 \\ -34 & -k\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

So, the correct answer is $|\begin{aligned}-14 & 11 \\ -34 & -k\end{aligned}|=-4|\begin{aligned}9 & 11 \\ 6 & -k\end{aligned}|$ only.

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3-10 \\  & -13.\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $x$ is given by $x=\frac{{D}_{x}}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x} & =|\begin{aligned}k & 5 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{D}_{x}}{D} \\ -1 & =\frac{|\begin{aligned}k & 5 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}|}{-13} \\ |\begin{aligned}k & 5 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}| & =(-1)(-13) \\ |\begin{aligned}k & 5 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}| & =13\end{aligned}
$$

So, the correct answer is $|\begin{aligned}k & 5 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}|=13$ only.

v:
Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement “$L$ is closed under matrix addition” is false. For example, if ${A}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ and ${A}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which is not a matrix from $L.$ So, $L$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement “$L$ is closed under scalar multiplication” is false. For example if $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $k=0,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kA & =0\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which is not a matrix from $L.$ So, $L$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement “$L$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$” is false, while statement “$L$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$” is true. $L$ is a *not* subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$L$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$” only.

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{9}{25}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{16}{25}} \\  & =\pm \frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =-\frac{4}{5}.$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{3}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{3},$ as follows:

$$

$$

The intermediate value theorem can be applied on closed intervals on which the function is continuous. 

The function $f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ is discontinuous at the values of $x$ which make the denominator $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ equal to zero. Therefore, $f(x)$ is discontinuous at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi $, where $n$ is any integer.

- On the interval $[0,1],$ we **can** apply the intermediate value theorem to $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$

- On the interval $[1,2],$ we **cannot** apply the intermediate value theorem to $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ because this interval contains the point of discontinuity $\frac{\pi }{2}≈1.57\,.$

- On the interval $[-1,0),$ we **cannot** apply the intermediate value theorem to $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ because this interval is not closed.

Therefore, the correct answer is $[0,1]$ only.

The invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\text{Col}(A) &={R}^{n} \\ \text{dim(Col}(A)) &=n=\text{rank}(A) \\ \text{Null}(A) &=\{0\} \\ \text{dim(Null}(A)) &=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}\right.$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $A$ has no inverse.* $\,✓$

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $\text{rank}(A)=n.$*$\,\times$

Since our matrix is not invertible, according to the invertible matrix theorem, it must be $\text{rank}(A)\ne n.$

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.*  $\,\times$

Since $\text{rank}(A)\ne n$, it must be $\text{dim(Col}(A))<n,$ which means that not all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$A$ has no inverse” only.

Recall that given $A=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

1\. $A$ is invertible.

2\. The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

3\. The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

4\. The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

5\. $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement $det(A)\ne 0$ is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det\begin{bmatrix}5 & -1 \\ -5 & k\end{bmatrix} \\  & =5\cdot k-(-1)\cdot (-5) \\  & =5k-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $5k-5\ne 0$ if $k\ne 1.$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement “$Ax=0$ has no solution” is false. According to the third part of the invertible matrix theorem, there must be a unique zero solution to $Ax=0.$

- Statement “The lines $5x-y=-1$ and $-5x+ky=0$ intersect exactly at one point” is true. According to the fourth part of the invertible matrix theorem, the lines must intersect at exactly one point.

Finally, only statements $det(A)\ne 0$ and “The lines $5x-y=-1$ and $-5x+ky=0$ intersect exactly at one point” are true.

Let $r$  be the radius, $A$ the area, and $C$ the circumference of the circle. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {\left(\frac{C}{2\pi }\right)}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}\left(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi } \\ \frac{2}{3} & =\frac{C}{2\pi } \\ C & =\frac{4\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $C=2\pi r,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi r & =\frac{4\pi }{3} \\ r & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cot}⁡(2t),$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cot}⁡(2t))}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)} \\  & =\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡(2t)}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}{csc}^{3}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate at $t=\frac{\pi }{12},$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}{|}_{t=\pi /12} & =-\frac{1}{4}{csc}^{3}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{12}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4{sin}^{3}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\cdot {\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{3}} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}

First, we rewrite the series so that it's in the form ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }a{r}^{n},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{kn-2}}{{9}^{n-1}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{kn}\cdot {3}^{-2}}{{9}^{n-1}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{9}\left(\frac{{3}^{kn}}{{9}^{n-1}}\right) \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\left(\frac{{3}^{kn}}{{9}^{n}}\right) \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{\left(\frac{{3}^{k}}{9}\right)}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that this is a geometric series with a common ratio of $r=\frac{{3}^{k}}{9}.$ 

For the series to converge, we require $|r|<1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\frac{{3}^{k}}{9}| & <1 \\ \frac{{3}^{k}}{9} & <1 \\ {3}^{k} & <9.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we could remove the absolute value bars because $\frac{{3}^{k}}{9}$ is always positive.

The equation ${3}^{k}=9$ has the solution $k=2.$ Now, since ${3}^{k}$ increases as $k$ increases, the solution to ${3}^{k}<9$ must be $k<2.$

We use the flowchart below to determine which tests to use for each series.

![](images/3a/3aa7f0243efeab51d00aa9694dd018245f7ca4664cc1a5fdf4e646aebb61536e.png)

With that in mind, let's test each series in turn.

- For the first series, we use the alternating series test. Observe that 

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{1}{n!}
$$

is positive and decreasing for all $n\ge 1,$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, by the alternating series test, the series

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n!}
$$

is also convergent.

- For the second series, we use the limit comparison test. Let 

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2\sqrt{n}}{n+2}\,{b}_{n}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

Working out the necessary limit, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n}}{{b}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{2\sqrt{n}}{n+2}÷\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}) \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{2\sqrt{n}}{n+2}\cdot \sqrt{n}) \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\left(\frac{2n}{n+2}\right) \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\left(\frac{2}{(1+\frac{2}{n})}\right) \\  & =\frac{2}{1+0} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $L=2$ is positive and finite. Now, the series

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

is divergent by the $p$-series test. So, the series 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\sqrt{n}}{n+2}
$$

is also divergent by the limit comparison test.

- For the final series, we use the $n$th term test for divergence. Let 

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{3}}{n+2{n}^{2}}
$$

Then, we have ${lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}=\infty ,$ since the polynomial in the numerator grows faster than the polynomial in the denominator. Therefore, by the $n$th term test, the series

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{n}^{3}}{n+2{n}^{2}}
$$

is divergent.

In conclusion, only series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n!}$ converges.

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $y=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{2}{4}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. Therefore $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$

Using the fact that $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta },$ we finally get

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}=1.
$$

The parameter $C$ represents a horizontal shift of the function.

First, we rewrite the function by factoring the horizontal stretch factor, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3x}{5}+C) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{5}(x+\frac{5C}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $x+\frac{5C}{3}$ indicates that the graph of $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{5}(x+\frac{5C}{3}))$ is a horizontal translation of $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{3x}{5}\right).$ Comparing the two graphs below allows us to determine the amount of this shift.

![](images/5e/5e9b6568ec493d95db6fe72a6a19024326c5b920629e9ff44a85db54089aa2a6.png)

From the diagram, we see that our curve has been obtained by shifting $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{3x}{5}\right)$ by $\frac{\pi }{3}-0=\frac{\pi }{3}$ units to the right. Therefore:

$$
\frac{5C}{3}=-\frac{\pi }{3}\,⟹\,C=\left(-\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)\,⟹\,C=-\frac{\pi }{5}
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $-\frac{\pi }{5}$ is in this interval, the value of $C$ is $-\frac{\pi }{5}.$

The asymptotes of $y=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ coincide with the zeros of $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ and are given by the following expression

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi ,
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

To find the asymptotes of $\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{3}),$ we replace the $x$ on the left-hand side of the above with $(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{3}).$ This gives

$$
\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi .
$$

Solving for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{3} & =\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi  \\ \frac{x}{2} & =\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi -\frac{\pi }{3} \\ \frac{x}{2} & =\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi  \\ x & =\frac{2\cdot \pi }{6}+2n\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{3}+2n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the expression giving all the vertical asymptotes is $x=\frac{\pi }{3}+2n\pi ,$ where $n$ is an integer.

v:
The range of $\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ consists of two intervals:

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{6})\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{6})\le -1,\,\operatorname{sec}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{6})\ge 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

- Multiplying the first interval by $\frac{2}{3}$ and subtracting $1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{sec}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{6})\le -1 \\  & \frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sec}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{6})\le -\frac{2}{3} \\  & \frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sec}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{6})-1\le -\frac{2}{3}-1 \\  & f(x)\le -\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Multiplying the second interval by $\frac{2}{3}$ and subtracting $1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{sec}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{6})\ge 1 \\  & \frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sec}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{6})\ge \frac{2}{3} \\  & \frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sec}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{6})-1\ge \frac{2}{3}-1 \\  & f(x)\ge -\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get

$$
f(x)\le -\frac{5}{3},\,f(x)\ge -\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the range is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,-\frac{5}{3}]\cup [-\frac{1}{3},\infty ).$

The domain of $y=\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ consists of all values where $\operatorname{sin}⁡x\ne 0,$ and is given by the expression

$$
x\ne n\pi ,
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

To find the domain of $-\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}),$ we replace the $x$ on the left-hand side of the above with $(\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}).$ This gives

$$
\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}\ne n\pi .
$$

Solving for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{6} & \ne n\pi  \\ \frac{2x}{3} & \ne \frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi  \\ 2x & \ne \frac{3\pi }{6}+3n\pi  \\ 2x & \ne \frac{\pi }{2}+3n\pi  \\ x & \ne \frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{3n\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain of the function is $x\ne \frac{\pi }{4}+3n\frac{\pi }{2},$ where $n$ is an integer.

The determinant of the coefficient matrix is

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =|\begin{aligned}2 & k \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $x$ is given by $x=\frac{{D}_{x}}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x} & =|\begin{aligned}-4 & k \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{D}_{x}}{D} \\ -1 & =\frac{|\begin{aligned}-4 & k \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}|}{|\begin{aligned}2 & k \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}|} \\ |\begin{aligned}2 & k \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}| & =-|\begin{aligned}-4 & k \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

So, the correct answer is $|\begin{aligned}2 & k \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}|=-|\begin{aligned}-4 & k \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}|$ only.

Since we want to find the projection onto the $xy$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $z.$ First, we solve for $z$ in the equation of the plane, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+y & =6\,⟹\,z=6-y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the expression for $z$ into the equation of the sphere, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =24 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+(6-y)^{2} & =24 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+(36-12y+{y}^{2}) & =24 \\ {x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-12y+36 & =24\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by completing the square for the variable $y$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-12y+36 & =24 \\ {x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-12{y}^{2}+18 & =6 \\ {x}^{2}+2({y}^{2}-6{y}^{2}+9) & =6 \\ {x}^{2}+2(y-3)^{2} & =6 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{6}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{3} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the projection of the intersection is the ellipse $\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{3}=1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4,2,1) & ={4}^{2}+3(2-1)^{2}-{1}^{2}=18\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=18.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+3(y-1)^{2}-{z}^{2} & =18 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{18}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{6}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{18} & =1\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}z-y & =2\,⟹\,y=z-2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the expression for $y$ into the equation of the sphere, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(z-2)^{2}+{z}^{2} & =8 \\ {x}^{2}+({z}^{2}-4z+4)+{z}^{2} & =8 \\ {x}^{2}+2{z}^{2}-4z+4 & =8\end{aligned}
