$$
{x}_{i}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{i}{x}_{i}(t),
$$

where ${\lambda }_{i}$ is a constant. This means that we can solve each equation independently. 

With this in mind, let's examine our systems.

For example, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=4{x}_{1}(t)+5{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$

- System $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=-2{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &={x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$ is *not* decoupled because some of its equations depend on more than one variable. Indeed, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-7{x}_{1}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=9{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{2}(t).$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 9 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}.$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =1$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 9 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 9 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}-2-1 & 9 \\ -1 & 4-1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-3 & 9 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3{w}_{1}+9{w}_{2} &=3 \\ -1{w}_{1}+3{w}_{2} &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=3{w}_{2}-1.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get ${w}_{1}=-1,$ and therefore

$$
w=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{t}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=3,b=-1,$ and $a+b=2.$

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -8 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}.$ 

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=3+4\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=3+4\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=\begin{bmatrix}-4\text{i} & -8 \\ 2 & -4\text{i}\end{bmatrix}∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2\text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3+4\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{(3+4\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{(3+4\text{i})t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\text{i}(2{e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)) \\ {e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}({e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}+\text{i}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}+\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{\text{i}t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}+\text{i}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =-2\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}-4\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-2\begin{bmatrix}5\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=\begin{bmatrix}-3\text{i} & 3 \\ -3 & -3\text{i}\end{bmatrix}∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & \text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{(-2+3\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{(-2+3\text{i})t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\text{i}(-{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ {e}^{-2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}({e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+\text{i}\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{t}^{2}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

$$

$$

Notice that $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)\ge 0$ for all $y\in [-\pi ,\pi ].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(y,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2}\right),$ and

$$
D={(y,\theta )\,:\,-\pi \le y\le \pi ,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y}\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′},\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f{f}^{′})^{2}+(f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2}\right),$ we obtain ${f}^{′}(y)=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2}\right).$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =2\pi {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2}\right))}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & -6 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement “Any $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values” is false. Since $A$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 2}\times {A}_{2\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement “The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}$ has one negative singular value” is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement “Any $5\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values” is true. Since $A$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 5}\times {A}_{5\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is “Any $5\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values” only.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2} & =x \\ {x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 9 \\ -12\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -8 \\ 16\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ -4 \\ 32\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above gives the system with the augmented matrix 

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -4 & -8 \\ 9 & -8 & -4 \\ -12 & 16 & 32\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -4 & -8 \\ 9 & -8 & -4 \\ -12 & 16 & 32\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & -4 & -8 \\ 0 & 4 & 20 \\ -12 & 16 & 32\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & -4 & -8 \\ 0 & 4 & 20 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2} &=-8 \\ 4{x}_{2} &=20.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=5.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
3{x}_{1}-4(5)=-8\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=4.
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{B}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}.$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=4+5=9.$

Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $L$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ 2x\end{bmatrix},\,x\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement “$L$ contains the zero-vector” is true. The coordinates of the zero-vector satisfy the equation $4x=2y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & =2y \\ 4(0) & =2(0) \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$L$ is closed under vector addition” is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 2a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}b \\ 2b\end{bmatrix}\in L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 2a\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}b \\ 2b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a+b \\ 2a+2b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a+b \\ 2(a+b)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $4x=2y.$ Therefore, $a+b\in L.$

- Statement “$L$ is closed under scalar multiplication” is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 2a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}a \\ 2a\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}ka \\ k(2a)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}ka \\ 2(ka)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}

which satisfies the condition $4x=2y.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

- Statement “$L$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}^{2}$” is false. Since statements “$L$ is closed under vector addition” and “$L$ is closed under scalar multiplication” are true, $L$ must be a subspace of ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$L$ contains the zero-vector”; “$L$ is closed under vector addition”; “$L$ is closed under scalar multiplication” only.

Given a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=3{u}^{2}+2v$ and $y(u,v)=u+2{v}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =6u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =4v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}6u & 2 \\ 1 & 4v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =6u\cdot 4v-2\cdot 1 \\  & =24uv-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(1,1)}=24(1)(1)-2=22.
$$

Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{5}$ into ${R}^{5},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,\left\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{5} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=5 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}\right.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement “$T$ is invertible” is false. Since $T(x)=v$ has no solution, we have that $v\notin \text{Im}(T),$ hence $\text{Im}(T)\ne {R}^{5}.$ According to the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{Im}(T)\ne {R}^{5},$ the transformation $T$ and the matrix $T$ are not invertible.

- Statement $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}$ is true. Since $T$ is not invertible, the invertible matrix theorem implies that  $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

- Statement $\text{nullity}(T)=0$ is false. Since $T$ is not invertible, the invertible matrix theorem implies that $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}$ only.

The principle of induction states the following: Suppose we have a sequence of mathematical statements $P(1),P(2),P(3),…,$ where

- $P(1)$ is true, and

- $P(k)⇒P(k+1)$ for every $k\in N.$

Then, $P(n)$ is true for every $n\in N.$

In this case, the general statement $P(n)$ we're required to prove is the following:

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{n}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5n \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The principle of induction states the following: Suppose we have a sequence of mathematical statements $P(1),P(2),P(3),…,$ where

- $P(1)$ is true, and

- $P(k)⇒P(k+1)$ for every $k\in N.$

Then, $P(n)$ is true for every $n\in N.$

In this case, the general statement $P(n)$ we're required to prove is the following:

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{n}=\begin{bmatrix}{5}^{n} & {5}^{n}-1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We start by proving the base case, $P(1).$ To do this, we substitute $n=1$ into both the left-hand side and right-hand side and show that they're equal:

We proceed using induction on $n.$

**Base Case**: We first prove our statement is true for the base case $n=1.$
For the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{1}=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and for the right-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}{5}^{1} & {5}^{1}-1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, our statement is true for $n=1.$ 

Next, we state our inductive hypothesis. Here, we assume that the given statement is true for some $n=k\ge 1.$

**Inductive Hypothesis**: We assume that for some $n=k\ge 1,$ we have

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{k}=\begin{bmatrix}{5}^{k} & {5}^{k}-1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We must show that $P(k)⇒P(k+1).$ Let's start by writing down $P(k+1).$ This is the first part of the **inductive step**.

**Inductive Step**: We're required to prove that

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{k+1}=\begin{bmatrix}{5}^{k+1} & {5}^{k+1}-1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\,\,(∗)
$$

The idea is to rewrite the left-hand side of $(∗)$ *using the inductive hypothesis* and apply algebraic techniques to show that this equals the right-hand side.

When proving matrix identities using induction, the key to unlocking the proof is to factor out one instance of the matrix, as follows: 

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{k+1}={\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{k}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Let's apply this technique in this case:

We write

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{k+1} & ={\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{k}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

By the inductive hypothesis, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{k}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}{5}^{k} & {5}^{k}-1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5({5}^{k}) & 4({5}^{k})+({5}^{k}-1) \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{5}^{k}\cdot {5}^{1} & {5}^{k}\cdot {5}^{1}-1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{5}^{k+1} & {5}^{k+1}-1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

as required.

Since we've shown that the left-hand side of $(∗)$ equals the right-hand side, our proof is complete. So let's write down our conclusion.

Therefore, by the principle of induction,
${\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{n}=\begin{bmatrix}{5}^{n} & {5}^{n}-1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$

v:
A variant of the principle of induction states the following: Let ${n}_{0}$ be an integer. Suppose we have a sequence of mathematical statements $P({n}_{0}),P({n}_{0}+1),P({n}_{0}+2),…,$ where

- $P({n}_{0})$ is true, and

- $P(k)⇒P(k+1)$ for every natural number $k\ge {n}_{0}.$

Then, $P(n)$ is true for every natural number $n\ge {n}_{0}.$

In this case, the general statement $P(n)$ we're required to prove is the following:

$$
{\sum }_{i=3}^{n}(2i+3)=(n+6)(n-2)
$$

We start by proving the so-called base case, $P(3).$ To do this, we substitute $n=3$ into both the left-hand side and right-hand side and show that they're equal:

We proceed using induction on $n.$

**Base Case**: We first prove our statement is true for the base case $n=3.$
For the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=3}^{3}(2i+3)=2(3)+3=9,\end{aligned}
$$

and for the right-hand side,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(3+6)(3-2)=9(1)=9.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, our statement is true for $n=3.$

Next, we state our inductive hypothesis. Here, we assume that the given statement is true for some $n=k\ge 3.$ 

Due to the base case, we already *know* that the statement is true for *some* value of $k,$ namely $k=3,$ so this assumption is valid.

**Inductive Hypothesis**: We assume that for some $n=k\ge 3,$ we have

$$
{\sum }_{i=3}^{k}(2i+3)=(k+6)(k-2).
$$

We must show that $P(k)⇒P(k+1).$ Let's start by writing down $P(k+1).$ This is the first part of the so-called **inductive step**, so let's write that, too.

**Inductive Step**: We're required to prove that

$$
{\sum }_{i=3}^{k+1}(2i+3)=(k+7)(k-1).\,\,(∗)
$$

The idea is to rewrite the left-hand side of $(∗)$ *using the inductive hypothesis* and apply algebraic techniques to show that this equals the right-hand side.

When proving sums of finite series using induction, the key to unlocking the proof is to write the last term on its own, as follows: 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{k+1}{a}_{i}=({\sum }_{i=1}^{k}{a}_{i})+{a}_{k+1}
$$

Let's apply this technique in this case:

We write

$$
{\sum }_{i=3}^{k+1}(2i+3)=({\sum }_{i=3}^{k}(2i+3))+2(k+1)+3.
$$

By the inductive hypothesis, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}({\sum }_{i=3}^{k}(2i+3))+2(k+1)+3 & =(k+6)(k-2)+(2k+5) \\  & ={k}^{2}+4k-12+2k+5 \\  & ={k}^{2}+6k-7 \\  & =(k+7)(k-1),\end{aligned}
$$

as required.

Since we've shown that the left-hand side of $(∗)$ equals the right-hand side, our proof is complete. So let's write down our conclusion. 

Therefore, by the principle of induction, ${\sum }_{i=3}^{n}(2i+3)=(n+6)(n-2)$ is true for all $n\ge 3.$

To prove a statement using induction, we use the following framework:

- **Step 1**: Base Case

- **Step 2**: Inductive Hypothesis

- **Step 3**: Inductive Step

- **Step 4**: Conclusion

In this case, the general statement $P(n)$ we're required to prove is the following:

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}2(5i-3)=n(5n-1)
$$

We start by proving the so-called **base case,** $P(1).$ To do this, we substitute $n=1$ into both the left-hand side and right-hand side. 

In our case, this gives the following:

**Base Case**: We first prove that our statement is true for the base case $n=1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{1}2(5i-3)=1(5-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Proving that the base case is true is usually straightforward. We simply calculate the left-hand and right-hand sides independently and show they're equal.

Next, we write down our **inductive hypothesis**. We assume that $P(k)$ is true for some $n=k\ge 1.$ To do this, we simply replace $n$ with $k$ in our original statement $P(n).$ 

In our case, this gives the following:

**Inductive Hypothesis**: We assume that for some $n=k\ge 1,$ we have

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{k}2(5i-3)=k(5k-1).
$$

Due to the base case, we already *know* that the statement is true for *some* value of $k,$ namely $k=1,$ so this assumption is valid. 

Then, we move onto the **inductive step**: We must show that $P(k)⇒P(k+1).$ We start by writing down $P(k+1).$ 

**Inductive Step**: We're required to prove that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{k+1}2(5i-3) & =(k+1)(5(k+1)-1) \\  & =(k+1)(5k+4).\end{aligned}
$$

The inductive step is where most of the work lies. The idea is to rewrite the left-hand side of this equation *using the inductive hypothesis* and apply algebraic techniques to show that this equals the right-hand side.

Once we've shown that $P(k)⇒P(k+1),$ the proof is complete, and we state our **conclusion**.

**Conclusion**: Therefore, ${\sum }_{i=1}^{n}2(5i-3)=n(5n-1)$ for all $n\ge 1.$

Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & -6 & 3 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Setting $x=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix},$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & -6 & 3 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\left(\frac{3}{2}\right){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$

v:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 0 \\ 5 & -3 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Setting $x=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix},$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 0 \\ 5 & -3 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & ↔{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 5 & -3 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -18 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -18 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\left(-\frac{7}{18}\right){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -18 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have $x=0.$ 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}z,\,z\in R.
$$

This implies that $B={\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
must also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}<0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=-4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-7y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-5t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/df/df61bf017441f2dc3e34253d89f98f42cce2ec1b27131b9204952b059e335af8.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$

$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: Notice that from the matrix $Σ,$ we can deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0$ without solving the characteristic equation.

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-5I & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-5I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-0I & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}-0\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-0I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A{A}^{T}$): Since the first singular value is not zero, and we know the corresponding singular right vector, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that 

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,‖{u}_{2}‖=1.
$$

 

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get a nonzero solution $\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the  second column of $U:$ 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$

v:
We start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{bmatrix}5 & -10 & 15 \\ -1 & 5 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{5}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}5 & -10 & 15 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to basis vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the reduced matrix has $2$ pivot columns (or alternatively, it has exactly $2$ non-zero rows). 

Therefore, 
$\text{dim}(\text{Span}\{\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ 5\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}15 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}\})=2.$

Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

First, note that the direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-t \\ 3t \\ t\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
-x=\frac{y}{3}=z.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement “$L$ contains the zero-vector” is true. Indeed, from the definition of $L$ we have that the point $(0,0,0)$ is in $L.$

- Statement “$L$ is closed under vector addition” is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}-a \\ 3a \\ a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}-b \\ 3b \\ b\end{bmatrix}\in L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}-a \\ 3a \\ a\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-b \\ 3b \\ b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}(-a)+(-b) \\ 3a+3b \\ a+b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-(a+b) \\ 3(a+b) \\ a+b\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $-x=\frac{y}{3}=z.$ Therefore, $a+b\in L.$

- Statement “$L$ is closed under scalar multiplication” is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}-a \\ 3a \\ a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-a \\ 3a \\ a\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}k(-a) \\ k(3a) \\ ka\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-(ka) \\ 3(ka) \\ ka\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $-x=\frac{y}{3}=z.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

- Statement “$L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$” is true. Since statements “$L$ is closed under vector addition” and “$L$ is closed under scalar multiplication” are true, $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "All the statements are true."

The invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\text{Col}(A) &={R}^{5} \\ \text{dim(Col}(A)) &=5=\text{rank}(A) \\ \text{Null}(A) &=\{0\} \\ \text{dim(Null}(A)) &=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}\right.$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $A$ has no inverse.* $\,✓$ 

Indeed, since $det(A)=0,$ the matrix $A$ can't be invertible.

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $\text{Null}(A)$ has dimension zero.* $\,\times$

Since $A$ is not invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{Null}(A)\ne \{0\}$ which, in turn,  means that $\text{Null}(A)$ must have a basis so the dimension must be greater than zero.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $A$ has less than $5$ pivot columns.* $\,✓$

Indeed, since $A$ is not invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{dim(Col}(A))\ne 5,$ which means that $A$ has less than $5$ pivot columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$A$ has no inverse”; “$A$ has less than $5$ pivot columns” only.

Let's examine each of our statements in turn.

- Statement “For any $A\in R,$ we have $(-1)\cdot A\in R.$” is false. For example,the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\in R,$ since $4={2}^{2}$ and $2\in Z.$ However

$$
(-1)\cdot A=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\notin R,
$$

because a negative number ($-4$) can't be a square.

- Statement “For any $A\in R,$ we have $2\cdot A\in R.$” is false. For example, consider the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ from $R.$ Then, we have 

$$
2\cdot A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\notin R
$$

because the $22$-entry of $2\cdot A$ is not equal to $1.$

- Statement “For any $A\in R$ and $\alpha \in R$, we have $(\alpha +1)A=\alpha A+A.$” is true. Indeed, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A=({a}_{ij})\in R,$ the entries are just real numbers. Thus, for any $\alpha \in R,$ we obtain that

$$
(\alpha +1){a}_{ij}=\alpha {a}_{ij}+{a}_{ij},
$$

and hence,

$$
(\alpha +1)A=\alpha A+A.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “For any $A\in R$ and $\alpha \in R$, we have $(\alpha +1)A=\alpha A+A.$” only.

v:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each of the eigenvalues separately. 

- For $\lambda =-5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 2 \\ 6 & 7\end{bmatrix}-(-5)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 6 & 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}+12{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 6 & 12 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-6){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain  ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

- For $\lambda =8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 2 \\ 6 & 7\end{bmatrix}-8\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-12 & 2 \\ 6 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-12{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-12 & 2 & 0 \\ 6 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-12 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=6,$ we get the eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}.$

Therefore, two linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix $A$ are

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $3.$ Therefore,
$\omega =3.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =3$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[(6D-9Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-(6C+9Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)]+9t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ 6D\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-6C\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-1$ and $D=-\frac{1}{2}.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X]=4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{{e}^{-2}}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{{e}^{-2}}^{1}\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\,|}_{{e}^{-2}}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X] & =4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X] \\  & =4(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}})-2(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}) \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}-1+\frac{1}{{e}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case,

$$
\lambda =0,\,v=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,w=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Thus, the general solution of the system is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix} & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}) \\  & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2t+1 \\ t\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that ${x}_{E}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ are equilibrium solutions of the system since ${x}_{E}^{′}(t)=0.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=\frac{1}{2}x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2} & -2y\end{bmatrix},$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={x}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2y.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})=2x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y)=0 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2})=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}2x & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{y}^{2}}{x} & 2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{bmatrix},$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{{y}^{2}}{x}\right)=-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=\frac{2y}{x} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{{y}^{2}}{x}\right)=\frac{2y}{x}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{2y}{x} \\ \frac{2y}{x} & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,1)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,1)=(-1)\cdot 0-2\cdot 2=-4.
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =4.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}-4\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -2{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $2$nd and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. On the other hand, from the first equation we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ 

So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ Computing $A-(4)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{3}I & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & -2 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}-(4)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & -6 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations whose augmented matrix $M$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 4 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The above matrix is already  in row echelon form.  It has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.  From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{2}(-4({x}_{3})-6{x}_{3}) \\  & =5{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}5{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, $P=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}=0 & ✓ \\ {u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1 & ✓ \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $U$ is orthonormal.

$$

$$

So, $V$ is not an orthonormal set.

- For the set $W,$ we get the following:

$$

$$

So, $W$ is an orthonormal set.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$U$ and $W$ only".

$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-25I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-0I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}.

The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2(xy-3) & {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix},$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2(xy-3)\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}.
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}xy-3 &=0 \\ {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get

$$
xy-3=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{x}.
$$

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-9{\left(\frac{3}{x}\right)}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{81}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ \frac{{x}^{4}-81}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-81 & =0 \\ x & =-3,3.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting these values into $y=\frac{3}{x},$ we obtain

$$
x=-3\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{-3}=-1,\,\,x=3\,\,\,\,\,\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{3}=1.
$$

Hence, $(-3,-1)$ and $(3,1)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-6)=2y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-6)=2x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})=-18y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2y & 2x \\ 2x & -18y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(3,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(3,1)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 6 & -18\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(3,1),$ we get

$$
H(3,1)=det({f}^{″}(3,1))=2\cdot (-18)-{6}^{2}=-72<0,
$$

Therefore, $f(3,1)$ is a saddle point.

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(-3,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-3,-1)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -6 \\ -6 & 18\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(-3,-1),$ we get

$$
H(-3,-1)=det({f}^{″}(-3,-1))=(-2)\cdot 18-(-6)^{2}=-72<0,
$$

Therefore, $f(-3,-1)$ is a saddle point.

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has saddle points at $(3,1)$ and $(-3,-1).$

$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(Q)$ is $\{{q}_{1},{q}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\}.
$$

Now, since the $4$th column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${q}_{4}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{{q}_{4}}=\underbrace{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{q}_{1}}+\underbrace{(1)}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{{q}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=\frac{3}{4}\cdot 1=\frac{3}{4}.$

$$
f:\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y{x}^{2}-1.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2})=2{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y{x}^{2}-1)=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2})=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{x}^{2}-1)=2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2{y}^{2} & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-1)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,-1)=2\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot (-4)=-12.
$$

For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt{2},\,\,-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}\}.
$$

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $\lambda (r,\theta )$ is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{M}{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{M}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{M}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}r\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{M}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}\cdot \theta {|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{M}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot (1-\frac{1}{2})\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi M}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{y} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{\pi M}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi }{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)-8\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $5.$ Therefore,
$\omega =5.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =5$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[(10D-25Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)-(10C+25Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)]+25t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)-8\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ 10D\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)-10C\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)-8\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=\frac{4}{5}$ and $D=\frac{1}{5}.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{4}{5}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\frac{1}{5}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y$ $=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t+ϕ)$ $+\frac{4}{5}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)$ $+\frac{1}{5}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)$

2\. $y$ $=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t+ϕ)$ $+\frac{4}{5}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)$ $+\frac{1}{5}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)+\frac{4}{5}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\frac{1}{5}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)$

Only solutions $y$ $=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t+ϕ)$ $+\frac{4}{5}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)$ $+\frac{1}{5}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)$ and $y$ $=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t+ϕ)$ $+\frac{4}{5}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)$ $+\frac{1}{5}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)$ match the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is $y$ $=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t+ϕ)$ $+\frac{4}{5}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)$ $+\frac{1}{5}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)$; $y$ $=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t+ϕ)$ $+\frac{4}{5}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)$ $+\frac{1}{5}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)$ only.

Recall that:

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Let's examine our sets in turn.

- The first set is *open* since it doesn't contain any point of its boundary (all the corresponding inequalities are strict).

- The second set is also *open* since it doesn't contain any point of its boundary (all the corresponding inequalities are strict).

- The third set is *neither open nor closed*. It contains some of its boundary points, for example, the point $(4,2).$ On the other hand, it does not contain some other boundary points, for example, the point $(4,0).$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\begin{gathered}\left\{\begin{gathered}(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\\\,2\le x\le 4,\\\,0<y\le \sqrt{x}\end{gathered}\right\}\end{gathered}$ only.

Let's verify the statements one at a time.

- Statement “The identity matrix ${I}_{2}$ belongs to $T.$” is false. The set $T$ contains only matrices $A=({a}_{ij})$ such that ${a}_{11}{a}_{21}+{a}_{12}{a}_{22}>0.$ However, for the identity matrix ${I}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have ${a}_{11}{a}_{21}+{a}_{12}{a}_{22}=1\cdot 0+0\cdot 1=0≯0.$ So, ${I}_{2}\notin T.$

- Statement “For every $A\in T$ and $\alpha \in R,$ we have $\alpha \cdot A\in T.$” is false. For example, let $\alpha =0\in R$ and $A=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}\in T.$ Then, 

$$
\alpha \cdot A=0\cdot A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},
$$

where the sum of the products of columns' entries is $0\cdot 0+0\cdot 0=0≯0.$ Hence, $0\cdot A\notin T.$

- Statement “The set is closed under scalar multiplication” is false. Since statement “For every $A\in T$ and $\alpha \in R,$ we have $\alpha \cdot A\in T.$” is false, the set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

The diagram shows a series RL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $8\,Ω,$ and an inductor of inductance $1\,\text{H}.$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RL circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=8\,Ω.$

$$
{V}_{R}=8I
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=1\,\text{H}.$

$$
{V}_{L}=1\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ in the circuit is

$$
6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)=8I+\frac{dI}{dt}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+8I=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+8{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-8t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))+8(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ (-2\alpha +8\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+(8\alpha +2\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2\alpha +8\beta &=6\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ 8\alpha +2\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{3}{17},$ $\beta =\frac{12}{17}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{17}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{12}{17}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-8t}-\frac{3}{17}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{12}{17}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-8t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{17}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{12}{17}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{17}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{12}{17}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(-\frac{3}{17}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{12}{17}\right)}^{2}}≈0.73\,\text{A},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

$$

$$

$$

Applying our formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{part} & =\text{percentage}\times \text{whole} \\  & =12.6%\times 19,500 \\  & =0.126\times 19,500 \\  & =2,457\end{aligned}
$$

First, we convert the percentage to a fraction:

$$
12.6%=\frac{12.6}{100}
$$

Applying our formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{part} & =\text{percentage}\times \text{whole} \\  & =12.6%\times 19,500 \\  & =\frac{12.6}{100}\times 19,500 \\  & =12.6\times \frac{19,500}{100} \\  & =12.6\times 195 \\  & =2,457\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $12.6%$ of $19,500$ is $2,457.$ Hence, Emma must pay $$2,457$ in taxes.

$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$

$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$

$$

Therefore, we have

$$

$$

Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $3.$ Therefore,
$\omega =3.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =3$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[9(D-Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9(C+Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)]+9t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ 9D\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9C\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-\frac{2}{3}$ and $D=0.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)-\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$

Only solution II matches the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the top side.

For the top side, we have $v=\frac{7\pi }{4}$ and $3\le u\le 6.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{7\pi }{4}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{7\pi }{4}\right),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{7\pi }{4}\right)),\,3\le u\le 6.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a parametric equation of the line segment shown below.

![](images/b9/b976e62862ba82dfd89ff28627239dd5b5d1be1144e257223c091f29a5729f89.png)

 

Note that the line that this segment lies on passes through the origin. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. The slope of the line is

$$
k=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{7\pi }{4}\right)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{7\pi }{4}\right)}=\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{7\pi }{4}\right).
$$

As a result, our line makes an angle of $\frac{7\pi }{4}$ radians with the positive $x$-axis.

- Statement III is true.

- When $u=3,$ we obtain the point 
$(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{7\pi }{4}\right),\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{7\pi }{4}\right)),$
whose distance to the origin is $3.$

- When $u=6,$ we obtain the point 
$(6\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{7\pi }{4}\right),\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{7\pi }{4}\right)),$
whose distance to the origin is $6.$

So, the endpoints of the line segment lie on the circles of radii $3$ and $6.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1}\}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}-\frac{6}{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3} & 2\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & \sqrt{6}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$

$$
