Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{3}$ into ${R}^{3},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)=\{0\} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Since $y=z,$ any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ z \\ z\end{aligned}]=x\underbrace{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{{v}_{1}}+z\underbrace{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{{v}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(T)=2.$ Finally, according to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since $Tx=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ has no solution, this means that $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\notin \text{Im}(T).$ Therefore, $\text{Im}(T)\ne {R}^{3}$ and, according to the invertible matrix theorem, $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0.$

- Statement III is false. Notice that $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 6 \\ -9\end{aligned}]\}=\text{Span}\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\}.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(T)=1.$ So, $T$ is not a bijection or, which is the same, $T$ is not invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon, $V$ the volume, and $A$ its surface area. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the volume $V$ and the surface area $A$ of the sphere. Since $A=4\pi {r}^{2}$ and $V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3},$ the relationship between $V$ and $A$ is

$$
V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3}=\frac{4\pi }{3}{\left(\frac{A}{4\pi }\right)}^{3/2}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{3(4\pi )^{1/2}}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}A}\left(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }} \\ {A}^{1/2} & =18\sqrt{\pi } \\ A & ={(18\sqrt{\pi })}^{2} \\ A & =324\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $A=4\pi {r}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4\pi {r}^{2} & =324\pi  \\ {r}^{2} & =81 \\ r & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $6$-periodic function $(L=3)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{3}.
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right))+x(-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)) \\ \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{2}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right):$

$$
\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,[-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}]+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{4\pi }{3}A &=-\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{4\pi }{3}B &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=\frac{9}{16\pi } \\ B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\frac{9x}{16\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right).
$$

$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ is orthogonal, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{R}x & =\overbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{{Q}^{T}}\overbrace{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}^{b} \\ [\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2} &=-11 \\ 2{x}_{2} &=10.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=5.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-4(5) & =-11 \\ 3{x}_{1} & =9 \\ {x}_{1} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1}\}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 8\end{aligned}]-\frac{24}{12}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 8\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3} & 4\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overbrace{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}]}^{A}=\overbrace{[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]}^{Q}\overbrace{[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3} & 4\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}^{R}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{12}\cdot {r}_{22}=\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\cdot (4\sqrt{3})=-4.$

The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}xy-{y}^{2}-1 \\ -{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+5\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-{y}^{2}-1)=y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-{y}^{2}-1)=x-2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+5)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+5)=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}y & x-2y \\ -2x & -2y\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}(1) & 2-2(1) \\ -2(2) & -2(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 \\ -4 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(-2-\lambda ) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-2,1.$

Finally, since we have two real eigenvalues with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an $\text{unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

Notice that

- the samples are independent,

- both sample sizes are "sufficiently large," i.e., $\ge 30,$ and

- both population variances are known.

As a result, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the difference ${\mu }_{1}-{\mu }_{2}$ between the corresponding population means can be written as

$$
({\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2})\pm E
$$

where 

- $E={z}_{\alpha /2}\sqrt{\frac{{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}{{n}_{1}}+\frac{{\sigma }_{2}^{2}}{{n}_{2}}}$ is the margin of error,

- ${\overset{―}{x}}_{1}$ and ${\overset{―}{x}}_{2}$ are the sample means, ${\mu }_{1}$ and ${\mu }_{2}$ are the population means, ${\sigma }_{1}^{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}^{2}$ are the population variances,  ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are the sample sizes,

- $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

Now, to construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate:

$$
{\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2}=65-63.5=1.5
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.90=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We also need to find the $z$-score value ${z}_{0.05}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{0.05})=0.05,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$
From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that ${z}_{0.05}=1.645:$  

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |

 

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
E=1.645\cdot \sqrt{\frac{{4}^{2}}{50}+\frac{{3}^{2}}{40}}≈1.214
$$

- **Step 3.** Construct the confidence interval:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 1.5\pm 1.214\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. The end-points of our confidence interval are $1.5\pm 1.214.$

- Statement II is true. All values within the confidence interval are positive:

$$
(1.5-1.214,\,1.5+1.214)=(0.286,\,2.714)
$$

- Statement III is true. Since all values within the confidence interval are positive, this suggests that ${\mu }_{x}>{\mu }_{y}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2})=\frac{2}{2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2})=\frac{1}{2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(2{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2})=2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(2{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2})=5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}} & \frac{1}{2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}} \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
f(a)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -11\end{aligned}],\,{f}^{′}(a)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

The linear approximation of $f$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

Substituting $f(a),$ ${f}^{′}(a),$ and $a$ in the equation above, we obtain

$$
f(x)≈[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -11\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}](x-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

$$
0+2+5=7.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}^{R}x & =\overbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 3\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{2} & 3\sqrt{2} & -5\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}^{{Q}^{T}}\overbrace{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}^{b} \\ [\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-10\sqrt{5} \\ -10\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2} &=-10\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{2}{x}_{2} &=-10\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-10.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}(-10) & =-10\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5}{x}_{1} & =10\sqrt{5} \\ {x}_{1} & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -10\end{aligned}].$

Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1}\}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{6}{12}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overbrace{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{A}=\overbrace{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0\end{aligned}]}^{Q}\overbrace{[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}^{R}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{22}\cdot {r}_{22}=\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\cdot (2\sqrt{2})=2.$

v:
The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}) & -2y{e}^{x}\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2y{e}^{x}.
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}) &=0 \\ -2y{e}^{x} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the second equation for $y,$ we get

$$
-2y{e}^{x}=0\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

Then, substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x-{0}^{2}) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2x & =0 \\ x(x+2) & =0 \\ x & =-2,0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $(0,0)$ and $(-2,0)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}))={e}^{x}({x}^{2}+4x-{y}^{2}+2)\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y{e}^{x})=-2y{e}^{x} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}))=-2y{e}^{x}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y{e}^{x})=-2{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}({x}^{2}+4x-{y}^{2}+2) & -2y{e}^{x} \\ -2y{e}^{x} & -2{e}^{x}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get

$$
H(0,0)=det({f}^{″}(0,0))=2\cdot (-2)-{0}^{2}=-4<0,
$$

Therefore, $f(0,0)$ is a saddle point.

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(-2,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-2,0)=[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-2} & 0 \\ 0 & -2{e}^{-2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(-2,0),$ we get

$$
H(-2,0)=det({f}^{″}(-2,0))=(-2{e}^{-2})^{2}-{0}^{2}=4{e}^{-4}>0
$$

Finally, since $H(-2,0)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-2,0)=({f}^{″}(-2,0))_{11}=-2{e}^{-2}<0,$ the function $f$ has a local maximum at $(-2,0).$

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,0)$ and a local maximum at $(-2,0).$

For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:\underbrace{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & {e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)={e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & -{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ -{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & {e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(0,0)=(-1)\cdot 1-{0}^{2}=-1.
$$

$$
1\le x\le 7.
$$

We need to find the critical points of $P(x)$ for $1<x<7.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{P}^{′}(x)=0.9{x}^{2}-7.2x+10.8.
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical points:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 0.9{x}^{2}-7.2x+10.8 & =0 \\ 0.9({x}^{2}-8x+12) & =0 \\ 0.9(x-2)(x-6) & =0 \\ x & =2,6\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to find which of $x=2$ or $x=6$ gives a maximum value of $P(x).$ To do this, we compute the second derivative:

$$
{P}^{″}(x)=1.8x-7.2
$$

Substituting $x=2$ and $x=6$ into ${P}^{″}(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{″}(2) & =1.8(2)-7.2=-3.6<0, \\ {P}^{″}(6) & =1.8(6)-7.2=3.6>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second derivative is negative at $x=2,$ the point $x=2$ is indeed a local maximum of $P(x).$

$$

Therefore, $x=2$ is the global maximum of $P(x).$ So, the profit is maximum when a single course costs $$\,2.$

Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${u}_{1},\,{u}_{2}.$ To extend the given set to an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{3}$, we need to find a third vector $x$ such that $‖x‖=1,$ and

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{17}}{x}_{1}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{17}}{x}_{2}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{17}}{x}_{3} &=0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{17}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{17}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\sqrt{17}\cdot {R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=\sqrt{2}\cdot {R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{s-t} \\ {e}^{s-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{s-t} \\ {e}^{s-t}\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}(-s+t+1){e}^{s-t} \\ {e}^{s-t}\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-(t+1){e}^{-t} \\ 1-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1-(t+1){e}^{-t} \\ 1-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-{e}^{-t}-t{e}^{-t} \\ 1-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=8,\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,\,{\lambda }_{3}=1.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{6},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].

V=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.707 & -0.707 \\ -0.707 & 0.707\end{aligned}]
$$

be the matrix of principal components. 

Then, applying the change of variables $Y=XV,$ we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are uncorrelated), and

- the features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in ${y}_{1}$).

$$

As a result, we have that ${y}_{1}=-0.707{x}_{1}-0.707{x}_{2}$ will contain most of the variance of the data. 

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

$$
{y}_{1}=-0.707{x}_{1}-0.707{x}_{2}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-0.5x+0.5xy)=-0.5+0.5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-0.5x+0.5xy)=0.5x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-5xy)=-5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-5xy)=1-5x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}-0.5+0.5y & 0.5x \\ -5y & 1-5x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0.2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}-0.5+0.5(1) & 0.5(0.2) \\ -5(1) & 1-5(0.2)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.1 \\ -5 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & 0.1 \\ -5 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-\lambda )-(-5)\cdot 0.1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=\pm 0.5\sqrt{2}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is $\text{a stable}$ $\text{center}.$

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model (as in this problem), it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues. 

**Watch out!** 
In contrast, for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone is inconclusive (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source).

Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=5$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=3$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{3-x},\,x=0,1,2,3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{3-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{3-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(3-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(3-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(3n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{3}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{4}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{5}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(3n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{2})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{3})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{1}) \\  & =3\cdot 3\cdot 1\cdot 3\cdot 3 \\  & =81,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S=2+1+3+1+1=8.
$$

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta )$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(81)+8\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(3\cdot 5-8)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(81)+8\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +7\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=81+8+7=96.
$$

First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}17{x}^{2}\cdot {9}^{x+5}+x\cdot {9}^{x+5}-5\cdot {9}^{x+5} & ={x}^{2}\cdot {9}^{x+5}+17x\cdot {9}^{x+5} \\ 17{x}^{2}\cdot {9}^{x+5}+x\cdot {9}^{x+5}-5\cdot {9}^{x+5}-{x}^{2}\cdot {9}^{x+5}-17x\cdot {9}^{x+5} & =0 \\ 16{x}^{2}\cdot {9}^{x+5}-16x\cdot {9}^{x+5}-5\cdot {9}^{x+5} & =0 \\ (16{x}^{2}-16x-5)\cdot {9}^{x+5} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
16{x}^{2}-16x-5=0\,\text{and}\,{9}^{x+5}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation $16{x}^{2}-16x-5=0$ can be factored as

$$
(4x+1)(4x-5)=0,
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-\frac{1}{4},\frac{5}{4}.$

- The equation ${9}^{x+5}=0$ has no solutions because ${9}^{x+5}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

The equation of forced harmonic motion without damping is

$$
{y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=18\,⟹\,\omega =3\sqrt{2}.
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\sqrt{2}t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\sqrt{2}t).
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=6{sin}^{2}⁡pt$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution, which is $\omega =3\sqrt{2}.$ Since 

$$
f(t)=6{sin}^{2}⁡pt=3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡2pt,
$$

the frequency of the external periodic force is $2p.$

Therefore, the oscillator experiences resonance when $p=\frac{\omega }{2}=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}.$

Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the first column must be orthogonal to the second column, and

- the norm of the first column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x+2y-6 & 2x+2y\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4x+2y-6,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2x+2y.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+2y-6)=4 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+2y)=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+2y)=2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(3,-3),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(3,-3)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(3,-3),$ we get

$$
H(3,-3)=det({f}^{″}(3,-3))=4\cdot 2-{2}^{2}=4>0.
$$

- Statement II is false. We have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)=({f}^{″}(3,-3))_{11}=4>0.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(3,-3)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)>0,$ the point $(3,-3)$ is a local minimum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

v:
The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}})=\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})=-\frac{2}{{y}^{3}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} & -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & -\frac{2}{{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(-1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-1,1)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(-1,1),$ we get

$$
H(-1,1)=det({f}^{″}(-1,1))=(-2)^{2}-(-1)^{2}=3>0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,1)=({f}^{″}(-1,1))_{11}=-2<0.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(-1,1)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,1)<0,$ the point $(-1,1)$ is a local maximum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

For synthetic division to work, we need the coefficient of $x$ in the denominator to be equal to $1.$ So first, we factor the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{2x+1} & =\frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{2(x+\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{(x+\frac{1}{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Carrying out the synthetic division process on $\frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{(x+\frac{1}{2})}$, we arrive at the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 8 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\  & ↓ & -4 & 0 & 1 \\  & 8 & 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{(x+\frac{1}{2})} & =\frac{1}{2}(8{x}^{2}-2) \\  & =4{x}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, our final result is

$$
\frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{2x+1}=4{x}^{2}-1.
$$

Let $r$ be the radius of the hailstone, $V$ the volume, and $A$ its surface area. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the volume $V$ and the surface area $A$ of the sphere. Since $A=4\pi {r}^{2}$ and $V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3},$ the relationship between $V$ and $A$ is

$$
V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3}=\frac{4\pi }{3}{\left(\frac{A}{4\pi }\right)}^{3/2}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{3(4\pi )^{1/2}}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}A}\left(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }} \\ {A}^{1/2} & =12\sqrt{\pi } \\ A & =(12\sqrt{\pi })^{2} \\ A & =144\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $A=4\pi {r}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4\pi {r}^{2} & =144\pi  \\ {r}^{2} & =36 \\ r & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

The given information tells us that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=10\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ So, substituting $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ in the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}10\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ 10\cdot \cancel{\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}} & =2x\cdot \cancel{\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}} \\ 10 & =2x \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, at that particular moment we have $x=5\text{ m}.$

Since $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\text{Col}(A) &={R}^{4} \\ \text{dim(Col}(A)) &=4=\text{rank}(A) \\ \text{Null}(A) &=\{0\} \\ \text{dim(Null}(A)) &=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}\right.$

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A)=n.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since 

$$
\text{Null}(A)=\{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ 2{x}_{1} \\ -3{x}_{1} \\ -4{x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}\,|\,{x}_{1}\in R\}=\text{Span}\{\,\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -3 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}\}
$$

 
we have that $\text{nullity}(A)=1.$

Now,  for the matrix $A,$ the number of columns is $n=4,$ so according to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ \text{rank}(A)+1 & =4 \\ \text{rank}(A) & =4-1 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since $\text{rank}(A)=3\ne 4,$ then, by the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{Col}(A)\ne {R}^{4}.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $\text{rank}(A)=3\ne 4$, according to the  invertible matrix theorem $A$ can't be an invertible matrix.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions.

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12\lambda m+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-6\lambda )(m-6\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=6\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{6\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{6\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{6\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{6\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda x}+B{e}^{6\lambda x}+6B\lambda x{e}^{6\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+6B\lambda {e}^{6\lambda } & =0 \\ 6A\lambda +B+6B\lambda  & =0 \\ (6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{12\lambda }+2B{e}^{12\lambda }+6(6A\lambda {e}^{12\lambda }+B{e}^{12\lambda }+12B\lambda {e}^{12\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+6(6A\lambda +B+12B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+36A\lambda +6B+72B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+(8+72\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+8(1+9\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+(8+72\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}6\lambda  & 1+6\lambda  \\ 1+36\lambda  & 8+72\lambda \end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6\lambda (8+72\lambda )-(1+6\lambda )(1+36\lambda ) & =0 \\ 48\lambda +432{\lambda }^{2}-(1+42\lambda +216{\lambda }^{2}) & =0 \\ 216{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda +1)(18\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{18}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x/2}+Bx{e}^{-x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0
$$

we get

$$
-\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{1}{2}B=0
$$

which gives $A=B,$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =B{e}^{-x/2}+Bx{e}^{-x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{-x/2}(x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{18},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/3}+Bx{e}^{x/3}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0
$$

we get

$$
\frac{1}{3}A+\frac{4}{3}B=0\,⇒\,A=-4B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-4B{e}^{x/3}+Bx{e}^{x/3} \\  & =B{e}^{x/3}(x-4) \\  & =C{e}^{x/3}(x-4)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x/2}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/3}(x-4).$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-8\sin(2t-\frac{2\pi}{3}),\,{y}^{′}(t)=8\cos(2t-\frac{2\pi}{3})
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
8\cos(2t-\frac{2\pi}{3})=0\,⟹\,t=\frac{7\pi}{12}, \frac{13\pi}{12}, \frac{19\pi}{12}, \frac{25\pi}{12}.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}\left(\frac{7\pi}{12}\right) & =-8\ne 0, \\ {x}^{′}\left(\frac{13\pi}{12}\right) & =8\ne 0, \\ {x}^{′}\left(\frac{19\pi}{12}\right) & =-8\ne 0, \\ {x}^{′}\left(\frac{25\pi}{12}\right) & =8\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed vertical when $t=\frac{7\pi}{12}, \frac{13\pi}{12}, \frac{19\pi}{12}, \frac{25\pi}{12}.$

At a given point, a function $f(x,y,z)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\ln (x^{3}y^{2}z^{4})),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\ln (x^{3}y^{2}z^{4})),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}(\ln (x^{3}y^{2}z^{4}))⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{1}{x^{3}y^{2}z^{4}}\cdot 3x^{2}y^{2}z^{4},\,\frac{1}{x^{3}y^{2}z^{4}}\cdot 2x^{3}y^{1}z^{4},\,\frac{1}{x^{3}y^{2}z^{4}}\cdot 4x^{3}y^{2}z^{3}⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{3}{x},\,\frac{2}{y},\,\frac{4}{z}⟩ \\ ∇f(1,1,1) & =⟨\frac{3}{1},\,\frac{2}{1},\,\frac{4}{1}⟩ \\ & =⟨3,\,2,\,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding unit direction is

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{∇f(1,1,1)}{‖∇f(1,1,1)‖} \\ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(2)^{2}+(4)^{2}}}⟨3,\,2,\,4⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{3 \sqrt{29}}{29},\,\frac{2 \sqrt{29}}{29},\,\frac{4 \sqrt{29}}{29}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the unit direction of $⟨\frac{3 \sqrt{29}}{29},\,\frac{2 \sqrt{29}}{29},\,\frac{4 \sqrt{29}}{29}⟩.$

We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=3$, we have ${\omega }_{3}=\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{3}=\omega ,$ the $n=3$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=3$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{3}(x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{3}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right))+x(-\frac{3\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right)+\frac{3\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″} & =-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right)+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right)-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{3}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right):$

$$
[-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right)+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right)-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{3}}]+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right)+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-3\pi A=0 \\ 3\pi B=\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=0 \\ B=\frac{1}{27\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{x}{27\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form

must also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4y(t)\end{aligned}

Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=10$ independent random variables with unknown parameter $\theta ,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x)=\theta {x}^{-\theta -1},\,x\ge 1.
$$

For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:\underbrace{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2}-2x & 2y{x}^{2}\end{aligned}],$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2}-2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y{x}^{2}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}-2x)=2{y}^{2}-2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y{x}^{2})=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}-2x)=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{x}^{2})=2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-2 & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-1)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,-1)=0\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot (-4)=-16.
$$

$$

So, we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point $(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,\frac{\pi }{6}} & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m:$

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{3}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=\sqrt{3}.$ We get

$$

The normal crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at  $(0,\,-4).$

$\sum a{r}^{n}.$

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{4},$ and so the sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of this geometric series is given by

Since $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\text{Col}(A) &={R}^{3} \\ \text{dim(Col}(A)) &=3=\text{rank}(A) \\ \text{Null}(A) &=\{0\} \\ \text{dim(Null}(A)) &=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}\right.$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn. 

- Statement I is false. Indeed,   a matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$ Since here we have $det(A)=-1\ne 0,$ our matrix $A$ must be invertible.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, by the invertible matrix theorem
$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\text{rank}(A)=3.$

- Statement III is false. Since $\text{rank}(A)=3$,  it must be $\text{dim(Col}(A))=3$ which, in turn, means that  $A$ has $3$ pivot columns, not $4.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

The invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\text{Col}(A) &={R}^{n} \\ \text{dim(Col}(A)) &=n=\text{rank}(A) \\ \text{Null}(A) &=\{0\} \\ \text{dim(Null}(A)) &=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}\right.$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately. 

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $\text{Null}(A)$ has no basis.* $\,\times$ 

Since $\text{nullity}(A)\ne 0,$ we have $\text{Null}(A)\ne \{0\}$ which, in turn, means that $\text{Null}(A)$ must have a basis.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $A$ is **not** invertible.* $\,✓$

Indeed, by the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{nullity}(A)\ne 0,$ we must have that $A$ is **not** invertible.

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.* $\,\times$

Since $A$ is not invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{Col}(A)\ne {R}^{n},$ which means that not all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt[4]{6}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{4})=\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{(\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+\frac{16}{3}{t}^{6}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}(1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\cdot 2|t|\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}

The center of the expansion is $x=6,$ and since the series is convergent for $x=\frac{5}{2},$ this means that the radius of convergence $R$ is *at least* $\frac{7}{2},$ i.e., $R\ge \frac{7}{2}.$ So, the series is convergent for every point in the interval $[\frac{5}{2},\frac{19}{2}).$ However, we know nothing about the convergence of the series at any point outside the interval $[\frac{5}{2},\frac{19}{2}).$

![](images/f7/f7b2a20d097d3ff34f92ff7f0015c449150575420dd53132d0b2703567628ef5.png)

 

With this in mind, let's check each of our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $2\notin [\frac{5}{2},\frac{19}{2}),$ we cannot guarantee that the series is convergent at $x=2.$

- Statement II is true. Since $4\in [\frac{5}{2},\frac{19}{2}),$ the series is convergent at $x=4.$

- Statement III is false. Since $\frac{7}{2}\in [\frac{5}{2},\frac{19}{2}),$ the series is convergent at $x=\frac{7}{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}5-5 & 0 \\ -1 & 5-5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0 \\ -1{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=-1.

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

$$

$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}+{w}_{2}=-1 \\ -{w}_{1}-{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=-1-{w}_{2}.

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get ${w}_{1}=-1,$ and therefore

We write the position of a point (vector) in spherical polar coordinates as $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ),$ where 

- $\rho \ge 0$ is the distance from the point to the origin,

- $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ is the angle between the point and the positive $x$-axis, and

- $ϕ\in [0,\pi ]$ is the angle the corresponding vector makes with the positive $z$-axis.

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then:

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=13$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-3I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 3 & 12\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=9,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2,\,{\lambda }_{3}=1.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=9:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-9I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 & 0 \\ -4 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-9[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -4 & 0 \\ -4 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-9I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=Ax-b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)={y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}({y}^{T}y)=2y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}=2{y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=Ax-b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}={\sum }_{j=1}^{2}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}={x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}{x}_{j}..\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is $2$ times the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=2y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}],$ we get

The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=Ax-b\in {R}^{3}.$ Then, $L(A)={y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{3}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}({y}^{T}y)=2y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}=2{y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=Ax-b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}={\sum }_{j=1}^{2}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}={x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{3}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

v:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n+1}}{(9+5n)^{n}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\left(\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n+1}}{(9+5n)^{n}}\right)}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\left(\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n}\cdot n}{(9+5n)^{n}}\right)}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{5n\sqrt[n]{n}}{9+5n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\sqrt[n]{n}\cdot \frac{5n}{n})}{(\frac{9}{n}+\frac{5n}{n})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{5\sqrt[n]{n}}{(\frac{9}{n}+5)} \\  & =\frac{5\cdot 1}{0+5} \\  & =\frac{5}{5} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{n}=1.
$$

Since $L=1,$ the root test gives no conclusion.

$$
\begin{aligned}100{x}^{2} & =7 \\ 100{x}^{2}-7 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the difference of squares formula, we factor the left-hand side of our quadratic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}100{x}^{2}-7 & =0 \\ (10x)^{2}-{(\sqrt{7})}^{2} & =0 \\ (10x-\sqrt{7})(10x+\sqrt{7}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the zero product rule, we have

$$
10x-\sqrt{7}=0\,\text{or}\,10x+\sqrt{7}=0.
$$

Then, we solve each equation separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}10x-\sqrt{7} & =0 & \, & \, & 10x+\sqrt{7} & =0 \\ 10x & =\sqrt{7} & \, & \, & 10x & =-\sqrt{7} \\ x & =\frac{\sqrt{7}}{10} & \, & \, & x & =-\frac{\sqrt{7}}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-\frac{\sqrt{7}}{10},\frac{\sqrt{7}}{10}.$ We can write this even more concisely as $x=\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{10}.$

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=0\,⟹\,x=\pi n,
$$

where $n$ is an integer. We discard all solutions except $x=\pi ,$ since it is the only value that belongs to the given interval.

So, the critical points are $x=\pi $ and the endpoints $x=\frac{\pi }{2},\,\frac{3\pi }{2}$ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints).

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=0 \\ f(\pi ) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )=1 \\ f\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)=0\end{aligned}

Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{(10n)^{n}n}{(8n+1)^{n}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\left(\frac{(10n)^{n}n}{(8n+1)^{n}}\right)}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\left(\frac{10n\sqrt[n]{n}}{8n+1}\right) \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{10n\sqrt[n]{n}}{n(8+\frac{1}{n})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{10\sqrt[n]{n}}{(8+\frac{1}{n})} \\  & =\frac{10\cdot 1}{8+0} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{n}=1.
$$

Since $L=\frac{5}{4}>1,$ the series diverges by the root test.

$$

We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=Ax-2b.$ Then, $L(x)={y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={\left(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T}={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T}\cdot {\left(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{T}y)=2{y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-2b)=A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T}\cdot {\left(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y \\  & =2\cdot {A}^{T}(Ax-2b) \\  & =2\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}([\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]) \\  & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}11 \\ 3 \\ 9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ 10\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 \\ -3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}58 \\ 26\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2}.$ 

Now, we need to find eigenvectors that correspond to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Computing $A-1I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are  orthogonal. So, we divide ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ by their respective norms to obtain the first and second columns of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖} & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x) \\ \frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x & =-{x}^{3}+\frac{7}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x \\ 3{x}^{2}+5x & =-2{x}^{3}+7{x}^{2}+5x \\ 2{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}(x-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $x=0$ and $x=2.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2.$

Now, let's draw our usual vertical arrow through the region to determine the lower and upper functions.

![](images/d1/d19b70836b7b377c498fa505868563115706b588b0a2216d09c6ec738f746bbd.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=f(x)=\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=g(x)=-{x}^{3}+\frac{7}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

$$

$$

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $x=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{\left(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{5}{9}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{4}{9}} \\  & =\pm \frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{2}{3}.$

$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ -3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

$$

$$

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1) \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$
